"You will learn to treat time not as an immutable constraint that binds you, but as a medium, a fabric you can grasp, fold, and reshape to your will."
The god paused, letting the magnitude of the power sink in.
The silence was deafening.
"And," Kaeleth added, the last words carrying a weight that made the very void tremble, "you will gain the capacity to stop time entirely."
Theo’s breath hitched.
"Not permanently," Kaeleth clarified quickly, sensing the instinctive recoil.
"Not in a way that would unravel reality."
"But at durations and scales that the designation’s development supports."
"Initially, you will achieve brief stutters and fractured moments of stillness within a limited radius around yourself."
"But as the designation develops, as you prove your utility... the periods will lengthen."
"The radius will widen until the world becomes nothing more than a frozen gallery of statues at your command."
Theo didn’t respond immediately.
He couldn’t.

His mind was already racing through the possibilities: the tactical advantage of a frozen moment, the ability to strike a killing blow while the target’s heart was suspended between beats, and the sheer, terrifying potential to dismantle Rex Rexilion while he was trapped in a single, eternal instant.
The power offered was godlike.
It was the power to rewrite the rules of the game that had broken him.
Slowly, Theo turned his head away from the God, looking one last time at his own timeline.
He looked at that pathetic, flickering line that ’nothing’ had been waiting for him at the cliff’s edge.
He saw the darkness, the inevitable collapse, the hollow emptiness of a life that had run out of meaning.
He looked at the void where his future should have been, and then he looked back at the burning fire of Rex’s signature.
’Better to die as a god’s weapon,’ Theo thought, a dark, vengeful resolve hardening in his chest like cooling steel, ’than to fade away as a footnote in his legend.’
"And after?" Theo asked, his voice cutting through the amber hum of the void like a blade through silk.
"After Rex Rexilion is nothing but a memory etched into a corrected timeline."
"What then?
What becomes of the weapon once the war is won?
Kaeleth turned his attention fully to him.
The God’s voice shifted, taking on a quality that Theo’s temporal awareness recognized as something terrifyingly rare: sincerity.
It was the measured cadence of a being making a vow, a promise that carried the weight of cosmic inevitability.
"Then," Kaeleth said, "the timeline corrects itself.
"The wound is cauterized...
The world stabilizes, returning to its natural rhythm, free from the gravitational distortion Rex Rexilion has imposed upon it."
"And you... you will retain the temporal domain’s designation permanently."
"You will remain the established Apostle of Time."
"For how long?" Theo pressed, his mind already constructing the terrifying architecture of such an existence.
"How long does this power last?
How long am I tied to you?"
"The designation’s duration is woven into the fabric of your own causality," Kaeleth replied.
"It is tied to the holder’s life."
"As long as you draw breath, the authority of Time remains yours to wield."
Theo closed his eyes for a moment, feeling the immense pressure of the offer.
"And what do I do with it?
After?"
"When Rex is dead, when the world has settled into its new equilibrium, and I am left standing there with this... this godlike perception."
"When I can see the seconds as physical barriers and the centuries as mere layers of dust."
"What becomes of a man who can perceive time as a medium but has no reason to move through it?"
"What you want," Kaeleth said simply.
"You will be the architect of your own eternity."
Theo opened his eyes and looked.
He looked at his own trajectory that flat, dead line that had promised nothing but oblivion.
He looked at Rex’s signature, that bloated, cancerous explosion of power that threatened to drown reality.
And then he looked at the cliff he had already stepped off.
There was no going back; there was no climbing up.
The fall had already begun.
His mind became a storm of fragmented memories, each one a sharp pang of what had been stolen.

He remembered his mother’s voice the way she spoke Rex’s name with that terrible, reverent cadence, the voice of someone who had already decided that Rex was the correct answer to every question the world asked.
The betrayal wasn’t just in the loss; it was in the acceptance.
He remembered Diana.
He could still see her standing on the training floor, her eyes fixed on Rex as he demonstrated some impossible feat of strength or skill.
He remembered the specific quality of her expression, that mixture of awe and something darker, something that looked dangerously like devotion.
He thought of Iris in the quiet, blue light of the early morning training sessions, the shared glances that meant nothing now.
He thought of Elaris’s warmth, a heat that now felt like a fading ember from a house that had already burned down.
He thought of the household staff, the way their deference had shifted, their eyes sliding past him to acknowledge the new hierarchy that Rex had constructed with terrifying ease.

chapters.title: Chapter 1037. The Gap Was Never Permanent, Just Unsolved
paragraphs: Twenty-nine years. Twenty-nine years of striving, of building, of believing in a system that was secretly being dismantled beneath his feet.
Twenty-nine years of climbing toward a summit only to find he was standing on the edge of an abyss.
But here, in this impossible place, the God of Time was offering him something that twenty-nine years of mortal effort had never produced.

He was offering him a variable. He was offering him the specific, mathematical possibility that the gap between them was not infinite and that the impossible could be made inevitable if the method was finally right.
Theo stood in the center of Kaeleth’s domain, surrounded by the swirling, hypnotic patterns of amber gold symbols that pulsed like the heartbeat of the universe itself.
He felt something stirring beneath his ribs. It wasn’t the desperate, clawing hope that had sustained him in his weaker moments.
Hope was fragile; hope could be disappointed. Hope could be broken.
This was different.
It was a profound, terrifying emptiness. It was the absolute ’nothing’ that comes when a man finally releases everything he was holding onto: his pride, his grief, his past, and his very identity.
He had let go of the rope, expecting to plummet into madness, only to find that the release was not a collapse.
The release was not a fall. It was a clearing.
He realized then that emptiness was not the enemy. Emptiness was not the worst thing that could happen to a man.
Emptiness was a canvas. Emptiness was a foundation.
From this void, from this absolute nothingness, he would build something that would tear Rex Rexilion apart.
"Yes," Theo said, his voice steady despite the storm raging in his soul. "I will do it."
There was no triumphant smile from Kaeleth. The God of Time did not perform satisfaction; he was too ancient, too woven into the fundamental mechanics of existence for such mortal displays.
He was beyond emotion; he was beyond approval. He was simply a function of reality responding to a new input.
Kaeleth extended his hand, or rather, he performed the precise gesture that communicated ’hand’ within the complex, nonlinear language of the temporal register.
Between them, the amber gold light began to churn and spiral, condensing with terrifying intensity. It became something that defied human optics, neither fully visible nor completely invisible.
It existed in that liminal state of something that was undeniably real but had not yet been granted the physical form required by the three-dimensional world. It was raw potentiality made manifest.
"The designation of the Temporal Domain," Kaeleth began.
His voice shifted. It was no longer the voice of a being speaking to a man; it was the voice of a being speaking to the very framework of reality.
He was addressing the divine operational code, the cosmic laws that governed all agreements.

He was stating a fact to the universe itself, a declaration that he was not violating any law because Theo had given his consent, and in the realm of gods, consent was the only operative condition required to rewrite fate.
"This power is given to Theo Morr Nightwing, who receives it freely and holds it for the purpose and duration defined by his will and the domain’s agreement."
The condensed amber gold mass moved. It drifted toward Theo like a predator seeking its mark.
When it touched his chest, there was no impact, no sound of flesh meeting force. It did not pierce the skin; it entered.

It was a nonviolent penetration that bypassed the biological entirely, sliding past muscle, bone, and blood to reach the layer beneath the fundamental register where the soul anchored itself to reality.
Theo felt it arrive.
It wasn’t pain. Pain was a biological signal, a warning from the nerves.

This was something far more profound and an overwhelming, terrifying quality of something becoming true that had never been true before. It was like being plunged into a room of absolute darkness and then having every light source ignited simultaneously.
The flash didn’t just illuminate the room; it illuminated the very concept of perception itself.
Time.
He could see it.
The word ’time’ had been a hollow metaphor for twenty nine years. It had been a concept, an abstract property of physics, a ticking clock, and a fading memory.
Now, the metaphor shattered. The illusion died.

He saw it as it truly was: a dimensional property of the universe, running in a continuous, inexorable flow. He saw it not as a sequence of events, but as the fundamental medium in which all things existed.
He saw the way movement was not merely a change in position but a ripple through the temporal fabric itself. The movement was the substance; the destination was merely an artifact of perception.

From where he stood in the amber void, he could see the entire timeline of Aethelgard laid bare. It was a vast, interconnected tapestry of cause and effect, stretching from the primordial dawn to the inevitable heat death of the universe.

And there, coiled like a parasite upon that tapestry, was Rex Rexilion’s temporal signature. It was unmistakable now—a jagged, cancerous wound in the flow of time, consuming causality, bending the threads of fate to suit its own monstrous expansion.
For the first time in all of those years of desperate, failing effort, Theo saw the truth. He saw the gap. He saw the distance between his own fragile existence and Rex’s overwhelming power.
But the horror of the previous moment was replaced by something sharper, something colder, something far more dangerous.
He observed the specific property of the designation he had just received. The gap was no longer a permanent feature of his reality.
The gap was no longer an unbridgeable chasm.
The gap was now simply a problem. And he finally had the tools to solve it.
Then, the sound broke through the sacred silence of the void.
It started as a low rumble in Theo’s chest, a sound that felt foreign to his own throat. Then it erupted into a laugh.
He laughed.
It wasn’t the laugh of a man who had found humor in the absurd, nor was it the laugh of someone who had discovered amusement in his fate.
It was something far more primal and terrifying. He had not laughed in six weeks, not since the last shred of his old life had been torn away by Rex’s shadow.

This laugh was the sound of structural failure; it was the sound of a man who had been compressed under the crushing weight of twenty-nine years of inadequacy until his very soul had crystallized into something harder, sharper, and infinitely more dangerous.
It was the release of pressure that precedes a catastrophic explosion.

Kaeleth did not interrupt. The God of Time simply let it run, watching with detached fascination as the last vestiges of Theo Morr Nightwing the man who struggled, who hoped, who grieved were burned away in that hysterical release.

When the laughter finally died away, it left behind a silence that was heavier than before. Theo stood panting, his breath coming in ragged, visible gasps that seemed to disturb the amber gold light of the domain.
His hands were clenched into fists so tight that his knuckles bled where his nails tore through the skin, but he didn’t seem to feel it. His face was transformed.

The exhaustion and the hollow grief were gone, replaced by something alien. He looked like someone who had walked through the fire and discovered that he was not made of flesh but of something that could burn.
He had arrived at the far side of the abyss. And he had found that the far side was not better.
It was simply different.
"I will go back," Theo said.
His voice was no longer that of a victim. It was quiet, carrying the terrifying stillness of a predator that has finally spotted its prey through the treeline.
"Yes," Kaeleth answered.
The God’s acknowledgment was the only sound in the vastness.
"I will find Rex Rexilion," Theo continued.
Each word felt like a nail being driven into the coffin of the old world. "I will hunt him through every second, every minute, and every fractured moment of his existence."
"I will find him where he thinks he is safe, and I will drag him into the present."
"Yes," Kaeleth said.
"And I will kill him."
There was no anger in the statement. There was no vengeful heat.
The words were flat, absolute, and terrifyingly certain, like a law of physics. It was not a desire he held; it was not a wish or a hope.
It was a decision that had already been written into the fabric of reality. He wasn’t promising to try; he was stating what would happen.
"Yes," Kaeleth said, the word echoing like a tolling bell.
Theo’s eyes, now reflecting the shifting amber currents of the domain, locked onto the gods. One final question remained, the one that had haunted his every waking thought since the cliff’s edge.

"And after?" Theo asked, the question carrying the weight of all the years he had lost, all the people he had failed, and all the emptiness he now carried as armor. "When the disruption is corrected."
"When the instrument has finished its work... What remains for me?"
Kaeleth’s form seemed to expand, filling the void with a presence that was both ancient and new.
"After," Kaeleth said, his voice carrying the promise of an infinite horizon, "is yours."

chapters.title: Chapter 1038. Notifications from a Man Who Doesn’t Sleep
paragraphs: The amber gold radiance of the domain suddenly intensified, surging upward like a solar flare. Inside Theo’s chest, something fundamental shifted.
The temporal designation wasn’t just sitting within him like a foreign object; it was nesting. He could feel it in his soul register a new, cold, and infinitely precise tool orienting itself.
It was the sensation of a blade finding its balance in a warrior’s grip, probing the boundaries of its own lethality, mapping out the parameters of what it could reach and what it could shatter.
It was hungry. And Theo was the hand that would feed it.
He didn’t hesitate. He reached inward, grasping for the most immediate, most visceral application of this new divinity.
The designation responded instantly, presenting its primary function to his consciousness with the surgical clarity of a weapon being unsheathed.
’Time Stop.’
It wasn’t the grand, universe-altering freeze of a god; it was something more intimate, more dangerous. A local rupture.
A brief, controlled severance of causality within a limited radius. But to Theo, it felt like holding the throat of reality itself.
’Test it,’ his mind commanded. ’See if you can break the flow.’
He willed it. He shoved his newfound authority outward.
The domain screamed not audibly, but temporally. The amber gold symbols that had been dancing in their eternal, flowing patterns suddenly jerked and locked.
The motion died. The universe didn’t go dark; it simply became static.

The symbols froze mid-spiral, suspended like insects trapped in ancient resin. Even Kaeleth, the eternal constant, found himself ensnared in the eerie stillness of a being caught between one moment and the next.
The God was still there, but the flow that allowed him to act had been severed.
’One second.’ The silence was absolute, a deafening void where even the concept of sound had ceased to exist.
’Two seconds.’ Theo felt the strain, a sharp, metallic tang in the back of his throat, the sensation of holding back an ocean with a single finger.
’Three seconds.’
Then, Theo released it.

The collapse of the stop was not a crash but a seamless reintegration. Reality rushed back in with a terrifying fluidity, as if the paused moments had never been interrupted but merely folded into the continuity.
The symbols resumed their dance; Kaeleth remained unruffled, though his eyes held a flicker of something new recognition.
Theo stared down at his hands.

In the physical world, they looked the same scarred, pale, human. But as he focused through the temporal register, he saw them for what they truly were: the soul signed physical extensions of a predator.
He saw the way his very atoms now hummed with the signature of the Apostle. In the soul register, the temporal designation wasn’t just present; it was integrated.
It was a living part of his intent, already coiled and ready, already orienting itself toward the singular purpose he had carved into his own heart.
He wasn’t just Theo Morr Nightwing anymore. He was the glitch in the system.
He was the error that would delete Rex Rexilion from existence.
He lifted his gaze to Kaeleth. His eyes were no longer those of a man seeking answers; they were the eyes of a man who had become the answer.
The emptiness he had discovered earlier had hardened into a diamond sharp focus. There was no more room for fear, no more room for doubt. There was only the mission.
"Send me back," Theo commanded, his voice carrying the absolute authority of a man who had already decided how the story would end.
Objectively speaking, the last month had been the most productive period of Rex Rexilion’s existence since his arrival in Erosyne.
It had been a month defined by conquest not merely of territory or power, but of the very souls of the women who defined the Nightwing legacy.

He stood in the rear courtyard of the Nightwing household as the first pale rays of dawn bled across the horizon. The morning air was crisp, carrying the faint scent of dew and damp earth, but Rex didn’t feel the chill.
He stretched with the slow, deliberate thoroughness of a predator who had been running a sustained, high-output operation and was now granting his body the grim acknowledgment of its own efficiency.
Every muscle coiled and released with flawless precision, a testament to the absolute control he now wielded over his own physicality.

Behind his eyes, the system’s notification queue hummed with the residual energy of his recent successes. The queue had been active since the previous night, pulsing with the confirmation of his most recent claim.
[PREGNANCY CONFIRMED Iris Morr Nightwing. Free Skill Selection unlocked.]
The first notification had arrived twelve days prior, a different kind of victory:
[PREGNANCY CONFIRMED Aurelia Nightwing. Free Skill Selection unlocked.]
Rex raised his arms above his head, staring up at the shifting colors of the sky. His mind wandered back through the month, dissecting his methods with the cold detachment of a strategist.
The training sessions with Aurelia had been... genuine. That was a rare commodity in his world.
He didn’t need to exert himself; his martial arts mastery made the performance of flawless, world-class instruction as effortless as breathing, but the value had lain in her reaction.

Aurelia was not some naive girl to be manipulated with empty theatrics. She possessed a perceptive function that predated any system ability: twenty more years of accumulated assessment, a lifetime of watching masters and frauds, and knowing exactly what real effort looked like.
She would have recognized a performance within seconds.
So, he hadn’t performed. He had given her real training.

He had pushed her body to its limits, watching the sweat drip from her brow and the fire ignite in her eyes as she grasped the true mechanics of combat. She had responded like an apex student, seizing the instruction with a hunger that matched his own.

Iris, however, had been a different challenge entirely. Her process was not one of technical mastery but of navigating the jagged wreckage of grief while simultaneously maintaining the deadly discipline of an assassin.
She was a woman who moved through the world with a blade in one hand and a memory in the other.

Rex hadn’t tried to push her grief aside; he had integrated it. His soul manipulation had revealed that Veylor’s soul anchor remained accessible within the communication window, a fragile, spectral bridge between the living and the dead.
Eleven days ago, when the window’s optimal conditions aligned, Rex had facilitated the impossible.

He had acted as the technical intermediary, the cold conduit through which Iris could reach across the veil. For twenty minutes, he maintained the soul level connection with the flat, professional precision of a surgeon.
He held the bridge steady while Iris spoke to the ghost of the person she had lost, allowing her to receive the words that grief had kept suspended in the air like poison gas.
’I didn’t listen,’ he reminded himself.
The thought brought no guilt, only satisfaction. He had granted her privacy because privacy was the currency of authenticity.
If it had been a clinical procedure, it would have been meaningless. By refusing to eavesdrop, he had made the experience real for her.

When she emerged from that conversation, she wasn’t the same woman. She was something new, someone who had taken what she needed from the dead and was now deciding how to wield it in the world of the living.
The system had quantified it immediately afterward. Her desire level had spiked to 78/100.
It wasn’t the absolute maximum, but it was a profound reading of the specific signature of someone whose deepest wound and deepest connection had been tended to by the same hand.
And that number had been climbing steadily ever since, tracked by the Desire Authority System as Rex continued his sustained, genuine engagement with her.
Two days ago, the climb had ended. The system had confirmed the maximum bond during a session that had been as intimate as it was transformative.
And last night, the system had delivered its final, undeniable proof of his dominion.
Rex let out a slow exhale, watching the steam of his breath dissipate into the morning air. The Nightwing bloodline was changing. It was being rewritten by his hand.

The symbols resumed their dance; Kaeleth remained unruffled, though his eyes held a flicker of something new recognition.
Theo stared down at his hands.
In the physical world, they looked the same scarred, pale, human.
But as he focused through the temporal register, he saw them for what they truly were: the soul signed physical extensions of a predator.
He saw the way his very atoms now hummed with the signature of the Apostle.
In the soul register, the temporal designation wasn’t just present; it was integrated.
It was a living part of his intent, already coiled and ready, already orienting itself toward the singular purpose he had carved into his own heart.
He wasn’t just Theo Morr Nightwing anymore.
He was the glitch in the system.
He was the error that would delete Rex Rexilion from existence.
He lifted his gaze to Kaeleth.
His eyes were no longer those of a man seeking answers; they were the eyes of a man who had become the answer.
The emptiness he had discovered earlier had hardened into a diamond sharp focus.
There was no more room for fear, no more room for doubt.
There was only the mission.
"Send me back," Theo commanded, his voice carrying the absolute authority of a man who had already decided how the story would end.
Objectively speaking, the last month had been the most productive period of Rex Rexilion’s existence since his arrival in Erosyne.
It had been a month defined by conquest not merely of territory or power, but of the very souls of the women who defined the Nightwing legacy.
He stood in the rear courtyard of the Nightwing household as the first pale rays of dawn bled across the horizon.
The morning air was crisp, carrying the faint scent of dew and damp earth, but Rex didn’t feel the chill.
He stretched with the slow, deliberate thoroughness of a predator who had been running a sustained, high-output operation and was now granting his body the grim acknowledgment of its own efficiency.
Every muscle coiled and released with flawless precision, a testament to the absolute control he now wielded over his own physicality.
Behind his eyes, the system’s notification queue hummed with the residual energy of his recent successes.
The queue had been active since the previous night, pulsing with the confirmation of his most recent claim.
[PREGNANCY CONFIRMED Iris Morr Nightwing.
Free Skill Selection unlocked.]
The first notification had arrived twelve days prior, a different kind of victory:
[PREGNANCY CONFIRMED Aurelia Nightwing.
Free Skill Selection unlocked.]
Rex raised his arms above his head, staring up at the shifting colors of the sky.
His mind wandered back through the month, dissecting his methods with the cold detachment of a strategist.
The training sessions with Aurelia had been... genuine.
That was a rare commodity in his world.
He didn’t need to exert himself; his martial arts mastery made the performance of flawless, world-class instruction as effortless as breathing, but the value had lain in her reaction.
Aurelia was not some naive girl to be manipulated with empty theatrics.

She possessed a perceptive function that predated any system ability: twenty more years of accumulated assessment, a lifetime of watching masters and frauds, and knowing exactly what real effort looked like.
She would have recognized a performance within seconds.
So, he hadn’t performed.
He had given her real training.
He had pushed her body to its limits, watching the sweat drip from her brow and the fire ignite in her eyes as she grasped the true mechanics of combat.
She had responded like an apex student, seizing the instruction with a hunger that matched his own.
Iris, however, had been a different challenge entirely.
Her process was not one of technical mastery but of navigating the jagged wreckage of grief while simultaneously maintaining the deadly discipline of an assassin.
She was a woman who moved through the world with a blade in one hand and a memory in the other.
Rex hadn’t tried to push her grief aside; he had integrated it.
His soul manipulation had revealed that Veylor’s soul anchor remained accessible within the communication window, a fragile, spectral bridge between the living and the dead.
Eleven days ago, when the window’s optimal conditions aligned, Rex had facilitated the impossible.
He had acted as the technical intermediary, the cold conduit through which Iris could reach across the veil.
For twenty minutes, he maintained the soul level connection with the flat, professional precision of a surgeon.
He held the bridge steady while Iris spoke to the ghost of the person she had lost, allowing her to receive the words that grief had kept suspended in the air like poison gas.
’I didn’t listen,’ he reminded himself.
The thought brought no guilt, only satisfaction.
He had granted her privacy because privacy was the currency of authenticity.
If it had been a clinical procedure, it would have been meaningless.
By refusing to eavesdrop, he had made the experience real for her.
When she emerged from that conversation, she wasn’t the same woman.
She was something new, someone who had taken what she needed from the dead and was now deciding how to wield it in the world of the living.
The system had quantified it immediately afterward.
Her desire level had spiked to 78/100.
It wasn’t the absolute maximum, but it was a profound reading of the specific signature of someone whose deepest wound and deepest connection had been tended to by the same hand.
And that number had been climbing steadily ever since, tracked by the Desire Authority System as Rex continued his sustained, genuine engagement with her.
Two days ago, the climb had ended.
The system had confirmed the maximum bond during a session that had been as intimate as it was transformative.
And last night, the system had delivered its final, undeniable proof of his dominion.
Rex let out a slow exhale, watching the steam of his breath dissipate into the morning air.
The Nightwing bloodline was changing.
It was being rewritten by his hand.

chapters.title: Chapter 1039. Someone Is Playing With the Clock
paragraphs: Rex rolled his shoulders, feeling the satisfying click of vertebrae realigning, and summoned the system interface. The translucent blue display flickered to life before his eyes, casting a cold glow across his sharp features. His first priority was assessing his war chest.
[Current Energy Balance: 50,000 points (Lustia’s bonus) + base encounter accumulation]
Three days ago, that number had appeared like a thunderclap. Lustia hadn’t visited his dream domain this time; she hadn’t bothered with the pleasantries of a full manifestation.

Instead, she had bypassed the passive communication channels and forced the message directly through the Mark, using the specific, urgent frequency she reserved for things that were too brief for a visit but too monumental to ignore.
Her message had been terse, almost reverent: "I counted... You are insane. Here is what insane earns."
Fifty thousand points. A staggering sum that represented more than just currency—it was a reward for audacity, a tribute to his willingness to tear apart the established order of Erosyne.
He had stared at that number for thirty seconds, not in shock, but in cold calculation. He didn’t celebrate victories; he weaponized them.
"Time to invest," he muttered, his voice low and hungry.

He bypassed the standard purchases and dove straight into the skill catalog. He had two slots open, two opportunities to rewrite his fundamental nature without spending a single point of his accumulated energy.
These were the rewards from the pregnancies of Aurelia and Iris, the physical manifestation of his dominion over the Nightwing bloodline.

His fingers danced across the interface, navigating past trinkets and minor buffs. His mind was already locked onto the two skills he had identified as his absolute necessities since his encounter with Lustia’s domain.
[FULL POTENTIAL ADAPTATION FULL POTENTIAL]
The description carried a weight that seemed to distort the very air around him. This wasn’t just a defense; it was evolutionary supremacy.
[ON FIRST CONTACT WITH ANY HOSTILE ABILITY, ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECT, OR DIVINE WORKING, THE SYSTEM ANALYZES THE MECHANISM AND INTEGRATES A COMPLETE DEFENSE AGAINST IT.]
[ALL SUBSEQUENT CONTACTS WITH THE SAME OR SIMILAR MECHANISMS ARE FULLY NEGATED.]
[ADAPTATION IS PERMANENT, CUMULATIVE, AND DOES NOT REQUIRE ACTIVE ATTENTION.]

Rex read through the terrifying scope of the skill. It covered everything: elemental magic, forbidden divine expressions, spatial distortions, and most importantly, soul-level workings that bypassed biological defenses.
The temporal clause sent a cold shiver of satisfaction through him: ’Time Stop, Time Loop, Time Reset all negated after first contact.’
’It won’t make me invincible immediately,’ he thought, a predatory smile touching his lips. ’The first hit will still hurt.’
’The first strike will still draw blood. But the second strike?’
’The second strike will be meaningless.’
Combined with his [Infinite Regeneration], he was becoming a paradox: a being who could endure any atrocity only to become immune to it.
[FREE SELECTION APPLIED NO COST]
[SKILL ACQUIRED: FULL POTENTIAL ADAPTATION]
The integration was instantaneous. He felt a subtle shift in his cellular structure, a new layer of metaphysical armor settling over his soul.
"Next."
He checked his inventory. His previous free selection, which he earned through Elizabeth’s pregnancy, had already granted him the skill [Dimensional Manipulation].
That gap was closed. He needed to find the second piece of the puzzle, the skill that would allow him to see the threats before they could even manifest.
He scoured the catalog, his patience thinning. There was nothing else at this tier that offered the strategic advantage he required.
He already had [Presence Manipulation] to control the battlefield and [Dimensional Manipulation] to control space.
Now, he needed to control information. He needed to see through the lies of gods.
There.
[DIVINE PERCEPTION FULL POTENTIAL]
[COMPLETE AWARENESS OF DIVINE SIGNATURES, DESIGNATIONS, WORKINGS, AND PRESENCES WITHIN RANGE.]
[PASSIVE FUNCTION: CONTINUOUS READ OF ALL DIVINE CLASS ACTIVITY IN THE ENVIRONMENT.]
[ACTIVE FUNCTION: TARGETED ANALYSIS OF A SPECIFIC DIVINE PRESENCE OR WORKING TO PRODUCE FULL OPERATIONAL INTELLIGENCE.]

The implications were staggering. This would allow him to track Apostle designations, identify patron signatures clinging to enemies, and most crucially detect temporal workings regardless of whatever masking techniques they employed.
No god could hide from him. No assassin could approach unseen.
He would see the ripple in reality before the blade even moved.
[RANGE: PASSIVE 500M, ACTIVE UNLIMITED WITHIN LINE OF SIGHT OR ESTABLISHED TRACKING ANCHOR.]
[COVERS: APOSTLE DESIGNATIONS, PATRON SIGNATURES, DIVINE DOMAINS, AND TEMPORAL WORKINGS.]
This was the eye of the storm. This was the ability to read the blueprint of the universe while everyone else was still trying to understand the rules.
[FREE SELECTION APPLIED NO COST]
[SKILL ACQUIRED: DIVINE PERCEPTION]
As the skill locked in, Rex felt his consciousness expand. The world didn’t change visually, but his perception of it fractured into a thousand new layers of data.
The air itself felt thick with invisible signatures, the faint hum of divine energies vibrating in the space between atoms.
He was no longer walking through a world of flesh and stone; he was walking through a web of power, and for the first time, he could see every single strand.

The integration of [Divine Perception] didn’t just change how Rex saw the world; it shattered his understanding of reality. It was as if he had lived his entire life in a silent film, only to suddenly be thrust into a roaring, multidimensional symphony of power.

The world around him didn’t just become richer; it became terrifyingly transparent. The invisible threads of divinity that stitched the fabric of Erosyne together were suddenly laid bare, glowing with a cold, analytical clarity that rivaled his own emotional insight.

He didn’t just see the Nightwing household; he read its divine signature like a text. He could feel the ancient, consecrated weight of the estate’s protection, a stubborn claim of ownership written in the language of the gods.
His gaze shifted outward, deeper. His mind peeled back layers of reality to read Aethelgard itself.
He saw the ambient divine presence, the accumulated, suffocating weight of eight hundred years of divine maintenance woven into the island’s foundational substrate.

It was a thick, invisible atmosphere of sanctified power. Running through it like veins of molten light, he identified the specific signatures of the Apostle network: distinct, colored threads of patron deities, each one a tether connecting mortal puppets to their celestial masters.
Then, he caught something darker. A scar in the divine register.

The residue of Kaeleth’s temporal working flickered in his vision, a ghostly, distorted fossil clinging to the island’s divine layer. Even after Lustia’s counter frequency had attempted to scrub it clean, the wound remained, a fading echo of something that had once torn at the throat of time itself.
’Everything leaves a trace,’ Rex thought, a cold smile touching his lips. ’Nothing is truly hidden anymore.’
With his new senses humming in his skull, Rex turned and walked toward the household’s outer gate.

The morning possessed that peculiar, melancholic quality of a month’s final day—the same sun, the same breeze, but carrying the subjective weight of an era closing. A month of conquest, of blood, of rewriting destinies.
He exited through the rear gate, stepping into the street that hugged the massive Nightwing outer wall. His boots crunched on the cobblestones as he turned toward the city center.
His mind was already shifting gears; the administrative duties of an acting combat director didn’t vanish simply because a month had passed. Power required maintenance, and he had a city to oversee.
He was approximately forty meters from the household’s main gate when the world suddenly screamed.
It wasn’t a sound; it was a violation.

The passive function of [Divine Perception], running at its baseline environmental read, suddenly spiked. The steady hum of ambient divinity was drowned out by a sharp, violent alarm that tore through his consciousness.
This wasn’t the background noise of history or the fading echo of a past spell. This was something raw.
Something immediate.
Something hungry.
An active divine signature. Not a trace, not a memory, but a live, pulsing presence that was tearing through the local reality.
His pupils dilated as the system’s read flooded his mind with data:
[WARNING: ACTIVE DIVINE SIGNATURE DETECTED]
[DESIGNATION: TEMPORAL]
[STATUS: ACTIVE / MANIFESTING]
The air around him began to vibrate with a nauseating frequency. The light itself seemed to stutter, catching on unseen gears that shouldn’t exist.
Time wasn’t just passing; it was being manipulated, twisted by an external force that was forcing its way into the present moment.
Rex stopped dead in his tracks. His muscles coiled instinctively, his heart rate steady despite the metaphysical earthquake threatening to unbalance his soul.
The tension in the air was so thick it felt like walking through water, each breath becoming a conscious effort against the pressure of a collapsing moment.
’Someone is playing with the clock,’ he thought, his jaw tightening. ’And they aren’t trying to be subtle.’

The hair on his arms stood up as the temporal distortion intensified, the very cobblestones beneath his feet seeming to age and decay in micro seconds before snapping back to their original state. The threat wasn’t approaching; it was already here.
Rex tilted his head back, his eyes narrowing as he looked up into the sky, where the fabric of reality was beginning to fray like burning silk.

chapters.title: Chapter 1040. A Ghost Walking Through a Photograph
paragraphs: The sky above Aethelgard did not merely change; it hemorrhaged. The morning light, once warm and predictable, began to fracture as if the medium through which it traveled had turned to cracked glass.

The atmosphere took on a sickly, unnatural quality, a visual distortion that signaled reality was no longer operating under standard physical parameters. The air itself felt viscous, resisting movement like invisible oil.

Through the lens of [Divine Perception], the true horror of the sky was laid bare. Rex didn’t just see clouds and sunlight; he saw the amber gold signature of Kaeleth’s divine authority tearing through the firmament.
It wasn’t the god himself, but a stolen fire—the specific, blasphemous investment of divine temporal power channeled into a mortal vessel.

The symbol was gargantuan, a celestial brand seared into the divine register. It hung directly above Aethelgard’s central district like the eye of a predator, claiming dominion over every second that passed beneath it.

Rex stared up at the burning sigil, his mind racing. His perception dove deeper, past the golden flames of authority, searching for the anchor the mortal soul that served as the conduit for this stolen divinity.
He found it.
The moment his consciousness locked onto the soul signature, a cold, flat sensation washed over him. It wasn’t fear.
It was the hollow, mechanical satisfaction of a predator whose trap had just sprung exactly as designed. Confirmation had arrived, but it felt different than prediction.
Prediction was a theory; confirmation was a cold, hard fact that demanded blood.
’Theo Morr Nightwing.’
The name resonated in Rex’s mind like a death knell. The boy was playing with fire he couldn’t possibly control.
Rex was still tracking the golden wound in the sky when the universe died.
The stop was absolute. It wasn’t a slow fading of motion or a gradual deceleration; it was a violent, instantaneous severance.
The ambient cacophony of the city—the distant shouts of merchants, the clatter of wheels on cobblestone, the rustle of wind—was cut off with the brutal precision of a guillotine blade.
One moment, the world was alive; the next, it was a corpse.

Pigeons were suspended mid-flap above the academy tower, their feathers frozen like carved marble. In the northern district, reconstruction crews became living statues, mid-swing with hammers that would never fall.

The water in the fountain behind Rex froze in mid arc, each droplet a suspended crystal suspended in a gravity that no longer applied. The silence wasn’t peaceful; it was deafening, a pressurized void that screamed in the ears.
Rex stood in the center of the frozen apocalypse, his pulse the only thing moving in a world of stone.
Immediately, [Full Potential Adaptation] roared to life.
He felt the attack. The temporal stop didn’t feel like stillness; it felt like an assault.
A metaphysical pressure slammed into his body, an invisible hand attempting to sever his personal timeline from the universal flow.

It felt as though his very existence was being unstitched, his atoms being told they no longer had permission to move through time. The sensation was nauseating, a psychic wrenching that threatened to tear his consciousness apart.
’This is it,’ Rex thought, his inner voice calm despite the cosmic violation. ’The first contact.’

The system worked with terrifying speed. In the seven tenths of a second between the moment the temporal authority struck him and the moment the adaptation completed its analysis, Rex endured the full, unmitigated force of the divine stop.
His nerves screamed as his timeline shuddered under the strain, the sensation of being ’erased’ from the moment threatening to overwhelm his senses.
But the system did not fail.
[ANALYZING TEMPORAL MECHANISM: DIVINE CLASS CHRONO SEVERANCE DETECTED]
[INTEGRATING DEFENSE... ADAPTATION COMPLETE.]
[TEMPORAL STASIS IMMUNITY GRANTED: SUBSEQUENT CONTACTS WILL BE FULLY NEGATED.]
The crushing pressure vanished. The invisible hands that had been trying to strangle his timeline suddenly lost their grip, sliding off him as if he were made of untouchable diamond.
The stasis still held the world around him captive, but Rex was no longer part of its prison. He was an anomaly, a living variable in a frozen equation.
A dark, hungry smile spread across Rex’s face.
The boy wanted to stop time? Fine.
Rex would show him what happens when you try to freeze something that refuses to die.
Rex took a step forward. His boot struck the cobblestone with a crack that sounded like a gunshot in the absolute silence of the frozen city.
Rex could move. The impossibility of it was a physical sensation, a low hum of defiance vibrating through his bones.
The temporal stop had struck him like a hammer made of absolute zero, delivering its first contact violation to his very existence, but the [Full Potential Adaptation] had already eaten the blow.

It had consumed the system, studied the divine structure of Kaeleth’s power, and created a lasting protection in Rex’s cells. The stasis still gripped Aethelgard, but Rex was now a ghost walking through a photograph.
He tilted his head back, his eyes tracking the descent.
Theo Morr Nightwing was dropping through the frozen sky. He descended with the terrifying, controlled intentionality of a predator who had suddenly discovered he could control the universe itself.
There was no fear in his movements only the intoxicating, reckless confidence of a boy who believed he had finally seized the leash of God.
Theo landed thirty meters away. The impact wasn’t graceful; it was violent.
The divine designation amplified his physical mass as he fell, and when his boots struck the cobblestones, the stone didn’t just crack; it exploded.
A spiderweb of fissures radiated from his feet, sending shards of granite flying like shrapnel. The sound of the impact was a dull, wet thud that echoed unnaturally in the silent city.
Theo stood up, his chest heaving, his eyes locked on Rex.
Rex didn’t flinch. He didn’t adopt a stance.
He simply stood there, a dark monolith in the center of a dead world, watching the boy crumble.
Rex had seen many faces on Theo. He had seen the flaring rage of the street punch, the suffocating shame of the formal apology, and the brittle, defensive pride of their sparring matches.
But this was different. This was something that had burned away all those lesser emotions.
Theo had surrendered his humanity to become something else, something colder, something hollowed out.
It wasn’t peace. It was a void.
It was the expression of someone who had already died inside and was now simply waiting for his body to catch up.
"You took everything," Theo said.
His voice didn’t carry the tremor of grief or the heat of anger. It was flat.
Dead.
It was the voice of an executioner reading a prepared indictment, devoid of inflection, stripped of hope.
"My house," Theo continued, each word falling like a stone into a deep well. "Diana... Iris... My grandmother..."
"And my mother." He paused, and for a heartbeat, Rex saw the ghost of the boy who had been broken before the emptiness swallowed it again. "The household’s respect. My position."
"My room."

Theo took half a step forward, his boots grinding the shattered cobblestones into powder. The amber gold light of the temporal sigil above cast harsh, hellish shadows across his face, making his eyes look like empty sockets.
"I had years in this world," Theo said, his gaze narrowing, piercing through the thirty meters of frozen air. "A lot of years of building something... It was slow... It was pathetic."
"It was unimpressive. But it was mine." His fingers curled into fists, the divine energy crackling around them like static discharge. "And you came."
"You didn’t just break it, Rex."
"You tore it out by the roots!"
"You left nothing but ash!"

sentences.text: The sky above Aethelgard did not merely change; it hemorrhaged.
The morning light, once warm and predictable, began to fracture as if the medium through which it traveled had turned to cracked glass.
The atmosphere took on a sickly, unnatural quality, a visual distortion that signaled reality was no longer operating under standard physical parameters.
The air itself felt viscous, resisting movement like invisible oil.
Through the lens of [Divine Perception], the true horror of the sky was laid bare.
Rex didn’t just see clouds and sunlight; he saw the amber gold signature of Kaeleth’s divine authority tearing through the firmament.
It wasn’t the god himself, but a stolen fire—the specific, blasphemous investment of divine temporal power channeled into a mortal vessel.
The symbol was gargantuan, a celestial brand seared into the divine register.
It hung directly above Aethelgard’s central district like the eye of a predator, claiming dominion over every second that passed beneath it.
Rex stared up at the burning sigil, his mind racing.
His perception dove deeper, past the golden flames of authority, searching for the anchor the mortal soul that served as the conduit for this stolen divinity.
He found it.
The moment his consciousness locked onto the soul signature, a cold, flat sensation washed over him.
It wasn’t fear.
It was the hollow, mechanical satisfaction of a predator whose trap had just sprung exactly as designed.
Confirmation had arrived, but it felt different than prediction.
Prediction was a theory; confirmation was a cold, hard fact that demanded blood.
’Theo Morr Nightwing.’
The name resonated in Rex’s mind like a death knell.
The boy was playing with fire he couldn’t possibly control.
Rex was still tracking the golden wound in the sky when the universe died.
The stop was absolute.
It wasn’t a slow fading of motion or a gradual deceleration; it was a violent, instantaneous severance.
The ambient cacophony of the city—the distant shouts of merchants, the clatter of wheels on cobblestone, the rustle of wind—was cut off with the brutal precision of a guillotine blade.
One moment, the world was alive; the next, it was a corpse.
Pigeons were suspended mid-flap above the academy tower, their feathers frozen like carved marble.
In the northern district, reconstruction crews became living statues, mid-swing with hammers that would never fall.
The water in the fountain behind Rex froze in mid arc, each droplet a suspended crystal suspended in a gravity that no longer applied.
The silence wasn’t peaceful; it was deafening, a pressurized void that screamed in the ears.
Rex stood in the center of the frozen apocalypse, his pulse the only thing moving in a world of stone.
Immediately, [Full Potential Adaptation] roared to life.
He felt the attack.
The temporal stop didn’t feel like stillness; it felt like an assault.
A metaphysical pressure slammed into his body, an invisible hand attempting to sever his personal timeline from the universal flow.
It felt as though his very existence was being unstitched, his atoms being told they no longer had permission to move through time.
The sensation was nauseating, a psychic wrenching that threatened to tear his consciousness apart.
’This is it,’ Rex thought, his inner voice calm despite the cosmic violation. ’The first contact.’
The system worked with terrifying speed.
In the seven tenths of a second between the moment the temporal authority struck him and the moment the adaptation completed its analysis, Rex endured the full, unmitigated force of the divine stop.
His nerves screamed as his timeline shuddered under the strain, the sensation of being ’erased’ from the moment threatening to overwhelm his senses.
But the system did not fail.
[ANALYZING TEMPORAL MECHANISM: DIVINE CLASS CHRONO SEVERANCE DETECTED]
[INTEGRATING DEFENSE...
ADAPTATION COMPLETE.]
[TEMPORAL STASIS IMMUNITY GRANTED: SUBSEQUENT CONTACTS WILL BE FULLY NEGATED.]
The crushing pressure vanished.
The invisible hands that had been trying to strangle his timeline suddenly lost their grip, sliding off him as if he were made of untouchable diamond.
The stasis still held the world around him captive, but Rex was no longer part of its prison.
He was an anomaly, a living variable in a frozen equation.
A dark, hungry smile spread across Rex’s face.
The boy wanted to stop time?
Fine.
Rex would show him what happens when you try to freeze something that refuses to die.
Rex took a step forward.
His boot struck the cobblestone with a crack that sounded like a gunshot in the absolute silence of the frozen city.
Rex could move.
The impossibility of it was a physical sensation, a low hum of defiance vibrating through his bones.
The temporal stop had struck him like a hammer made of absolute zero, delivering its first contact violation to his very existence, but the [Full Potential Adaptation] had already eaten the blow.
It had consumed the system, studied the divine structure of Kaeleth’s power, and created a lasting protection in Rex’s cells.
The stasis still gripped Aethelgard, but Rex was now a ghost walking through a photograph.
He tilted his head back, his eyes tracking the descent.
Theo Morr Nightwing was dropping through the frozen sky.
He descended with the terrifying, controlled intentionality of a predator who had suddenly discovered he could control the universe itself.
There was no fear in his movements only the intoxicating, reckless confidence of a boy who believed he had finally seized the leash of God.
Theo landed thirty meters away.
The impact wasn’t graceful; it was violent.
The divine designation amplified his physical mass as he fell, and when his boots struck the cobblestones, the stone didn’t just crack; it exploded.
A spiderweb of fissures radiated from his feet, sending shards of granite flying like shrapnel.
The sound of the impact was a dull, wet thud that echoed unnaturally in the silent city.
Theo stood up, his chest heaving, his eyes locked on Rex.
Rex didn’t flinch.
He didn’t adopt a stance.
He simply stood there, a dark monolith in the center of a dead world, watching the boy crumble.
Rex had seen many faces on Theo.
He had seen the flaring rage of the street punch, the suffocating shame of the formal apology, and the brittle, defensive pride of their sparring matches.
But this was different.
This was something that had burned away all those lesser emotions.
Theo had surrendered his humanity to become something else, something colder, something hollowed out.
It wasn’t peace.
It was a void.
It was the expression of someone who had already died inside and was now simply waiting for his body to catch up.
"You took everything," Theo said.
His voice didn’t carry the tremor of grief or the heat of anger.
It was flat.
Dead.
It was the voice of an executioner reading a prepared indictment, devoid of inflection, stripped of hope.
"My house," Theo continued, each word falling like a stone into a deep well.
"Diana...
Iris...
My grandmother..."
"And my mother." He paused, and for a heartbeat, Rex saw the ghost of the boy who had been broken before the emptiness swallowed it again.
"The household’s respect.
My position."
"My room."
Theo took half a step forward, his boots grinding the shattered cobblestones into powder.
The amber gold light of the temporal sigil above cast harsh, hellish shadows across his face, making his eyes look like empty sockets.
"I had years in this world," Theo said, his gaze narrowing, piercing through the thirty meters of frozen air.
"A lot of years of building something...
It was slow...
It was pathetic."
"It was unimpressive.
But it was mine." His fingers curled into fists, the divine energy crackling around them like static discharge.
"And you came."
"You didn’t just break it, Rex."
"You tore it out by the roots!"
"You left nothing but ash!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1041. He Broke My Jaw, I Broke His Whole Worldview, We’re Even (For Now)
paragraphs: Rex said nothing. His silence was not a refusal to answer but a predator’s assessment, a cold, analytical void that mirrored the emptiness in Theo’s eyes.
He watched the boy, not as a person, but as a phenomenon of collapsing grief and rising divinity.
"You did not even try to hide it," Theo said. The words were clipped and precise. "That is the part that I kept thinking about."
"You weren’t careful... You didn’t pretend to be anything other than what you are."
"You just walked into every corner of my life, and you dismantled it."
"You did it in front of me, and you did it without even bothering to look at me the way you don’t look at furniture when you’re rearranging a room."
Theo’s voice remained terrifyingly level. There was no tremor of rage, no crack of sorrow.
It was the flat, mechanical delivery of a man who had rehearsed his eulogy and his revenge until they became indistinguishable.
"You are a reincarnator," Theo said, the accusation hanging in the frozen air like poison gas. "You have a system."
"You have a patron... You have been operating in this world with every advantage a god touched interloper could dream of."
"And yet, you still felt the need to take mine."
Rex’s gaze remained fixed, unblinking. His mind was already running tactical simulations, calculating the energy output of the amber gold aura pulsing around Theo.
"I know what you’re thinking," Theo continued, taking another step.
The shattered cobblestones crunched beneath his boot with a sound like breaking teeth. "You’re thinking that I’m about to say something that confirms your worldview."
"That I’m the pathetic loser who blames the victor."
"That this entire performance is just my pride refusing to accept defeat."
Theo stopped. He looked at Rex with an expression of absolute, horrifying certainty.
"I am not performing," Theo said, and for the first time, a sliver of something sharp cut through the emptiness—a razor-edged clarity. "I genuinely have nothing left."
"That is the specific state I am operating from. Not anger. Not pride. Nothing!"
"And from nothing, I am going to do the one thing I have not done yet."
Theo’s right hand rose.
Through [Divine Perception], Rex saw it: the temporal designation on Theo’s soul wasn’t just active; it was hemorrhaging power.

The amber gold sigil burned with a blinding, unstable intensity, the divine authority flooding into Theo’s bloodstream like molten sunlight. The boy wasn’t just using power; he was becoming a conduit for a temporal catastrophe.
"I am going to kill you.
The declaration wasn’t a threat; it was a statement of fact.
Theo moved.

He didn’t run; he simply ceased to be thirty meters away and became present in Rex’s space. The temporal designation’s enhancement turned his movement into a blur that defied the frozen physics of the city.
He crossed the distance in less than a second, a golden streak of inevitability.
Rex’s mind screamed for him to move, to dodge, to pivot, but the calculation was incomplete. The strike was too fast, too absolute.
’Absorb.’
Rex’s instinct took over. He didn’t try to escape the impact; he braced for it, channeling his own internal energy to meet the blow.
The fist connected with Rex’s jaw with the force of a falling star.

It wasn’t just a punch; it was a temporal violation delivered through physical mass. The divine amplification didn’t just multiply Theo’s strength; it compressed the moment of impact into an infinitely dense point of force.

Rex felt his jawbone shriek as the pressure threatened to splinter it into powder. His teeth grated together with a wet, grinding sound, blood immediately flooding his mouth as his inner cheek split open like overripe fruit.
The force sent Rex hurtling backward.
He became a human projectile, tearing through the frozen air. He cleared twenty meters of street in a heartbeat, his body a blur of motion as he crashed into the Nightwing household’s outer wall.
The impact was catastrophic. The ancient stone wall didn’t just absorb the blow; it screamed.

A thunderous crack reverberated through the silent district as the wall’s structural integrity failed, sending a spiderweb of deep, jagged fissures racing upward from the impact point toward the crenellated edge.
Dust and ancient mortar exploded from the wound in the stone like shrapnel.
Rex slumped at the base of the wall, the world spinning behind a crimson veil. His breathing was ragged, each inhale tasting of copper and grit.
His jaw throbbed with a white-hot agony that demanded his attention, and blood trickled down his chin, staining his collar.
Slowly, deliberately, Rex pushed himself up.

His muscles burned, his vision flickered, but he sat up against the cracked stone, wiping blood from his mouth with the back of his hand. His eyes, cold and lethal, locked back onto the golden figure approaching through the haze of dust.

Rex tilted his head back slightly, studying the spiderweb of destruction above him. The crack in the Nightwing wall was deep, a jagged wound in the ancient masonry that wept stone dust like dried blood.
The impact had been more than physical; it had been a statement of intent written in broken granite.
His gaze drifted past the ruined wall, scanning the silent corpse of Aethelgard. The city remained trapped in its amber prison.
A pigeon hung suspended three feet above a rooftop, its wings frozen in a desperate attempt at flight. A fountain’s spray was a sculpture of motionless crystal.

The reconstruction crews stood like monuments to a forgotten civilization. Only two heartbeats disturbed the stillness: his own ragged breathing and the approaching storm that was Theo Morr Nightwing.
Rex reached up, his fingers brushing along his jawline. The skin was swollen, hot, and slick with blood.
Inside his mouth, the metallic tang of copper was overwhelming, and he could feel the grinding discomfort of teeth that had been forced together with enough pressure to shatter steel.

’First contact complete,’ Rex thought, his mind operating with the cold detachment of a surgeon. ’The temporal designation didn’t just hit harder; it compressed the moment of impact to maximize kinetic transfer.’
’The enhancement is a function of divine authority channeled through cellular mass.’
A faint, almost imperceptible hum resonated in his bones, the sound of [Full Potential Adaptation] finishing its work.
The system had already dissected the punch. It had mapped the temporal signature, understood the acceleration curve, and integrated the countermeasure.
The next time that fist connected, it wouldn’t be a violation; it would be a collision between two equal forces.
Rex pushed himself upright. His joints popped audibly in the dead silence.
He stood fully, tall and unbowed, despite the crimson smear running down his chin and the way his jaw throbbed with each heartbeat.
Thirty meters away, Theo had stopped.
The boy’s face had shifted. The hollow emptiness was still there, but it was now layered with something else: a flicker of genuine, startled recognition.
He looked like a child who had thrown a stone at a statue only to watch the statue stand up and turn its head.
Rex ignored the pain. He reached down and casually brushed the dust and stone fragments from his jacket with slow, deliberate motions.
He wasn’t preparing for a fight; he was preparing for an experiment.

His eyes locked onto Theo’s across the wasteland of frozen time. Rex felt that familiar, clinical spark in his chest—the specific intellectual curiosity that surfaced whenever reality failed to follow his calculations.
A variable had appeared. The model needed to be updated.
"You came back," Rex said.
His voice was rough and gravelly from the blood in his throat, but it carried no anger. No accusation.
Just the flat statement of an observer noting a phenomenon.
"Yes," Theo replied.

The word was short, but the flat delivery he had maintained during his monologue had fractured. There was a crack in his certainty, a minute tremor of something that sounded suspiciously like disbelief.
He had expected a corpse; he had found a survivor.
Rex took a half step forward, the broken cobblestones grinding beneath his boot. "You have a temporal designation."
Theo’s jaw tightened, his amber gold aura flaring brighter, casting hellish shadows across the street. "Yes."
"From Kaeleth," Rex said.
The name hung between them like a blade.

chapters.title: Chapter 1042. I Got Slow-Mo’d, Time-Stopped, and Ribcage-Cracked Before Breakfast
paragraphs: Theo’s expression fractured. For a heartbeat, the hollow void in his eyes flickered with something dangerously close to terror—the raw, primal recognition that the physics of his reality had just been rewritten without his permission.
"I read it," Rex said, stepping forward into the amber glow.
His voice was unnervingly calm, cutting through the oppressive silence of the frozen city like a scalpel. "The divine signature."
"The specific harmonic frequency of the temporal domain’s authority invested in a mortal vessel... I can see the way your soul bleeds gold."
Rex studied Theo with the flat, patient attention of a scholar examining a rare specimen. There was no malice in his gaze, no righteous fury, only a terrifyingly detached curiosity.
"I have been waiting for Kaeleth to make this move since I became aware of his operation... I simply did not predict he would choose you as his scalpel."
"Does it matter?" Theo spat.
The words were wet, choked by the grief that still sat like lead in his lungs. "Does it matter who gave me the power to erase you?"
"Yes," Rex said, tilting his head. "It matters significantly."
"Because you are not Kaeleth’s Apostle in the conventional sense."
"An Apostle is a chosen partner; an instrument is something owned, something used until it breaks."
"There is a fundamental difference in how the power responds to your will, and that difference is what will determine how this ends."
Theo didn’t answer with words. His right hand rose again, but this time the energy wasn’t just a blunt force; it was a shimmering distortion in the air.
Through [Divine Perception], Rex saw the mechanism engage. This wasn’t the absolute cessation of the Time Stop; this was something more insidious.

A temporal deceleration is a field designed to drag the target’s subjective experience through molasses, reducing their reaction time to near zero while leaving them conscious enough to feel every second of their own helplessness.
The working struck Rex like an invisible wave of viscous liquid.
For seven tenths of a second, Rex’s world turned to sludge. He felt his own synapses fire with agonizing slowness, his limbs feeling as though they were encased in cooling concrete.
His heart beat once, a thunderous, delayed sound that seemed to take an eternity to complete.

But in that same span, [Full Potential Adaptation] was screaming through his nervous system. It seized the temporal distortion, dissected its mathematical framework, and rewrote Rex’s cellular resistance in real time.
By the eighth tenth of a second, the sludge evaporated. Rex’s movement snapped back to full velocity as if the universe had suddenly remembered he existed.
Rex looked at Theo.

The boy stood frozen mid-gesture, his face twisted in a mask of horrified confusion. He had thrown what should have been an inescapable prison, only to watch Rex walk through it as if it were nothing more than morning mist.
"The Time Stop worked on the first contact," Rex said, his voice carrying across the cobblestones with deadly clarity. "The Slow worked on the first contact."
"The mathematical certainty of your designation means that everything you possess will work perfectly exactly once."
Rex’s eyes darkened, locking onto Theo’s with the inevitability of a guillotine blade. "You have one of each... And you’ve already spent them."
"AAAAAAAGGHH!"
The scream that tore from Theo’s throat wasn’t a battle cry. It was a sound of pure, unadulterated psychological collapse.

It was the sound of a dam breaking the uncontrolled release of three years of grief, loss, and humiliation that had been held at bay by nothing but sheer, brittle willpower. The dam had failed, and the flood was consuming him.
Theo lunged. He abandoned all technique, all finesse, and all restraint.
He came at Rex with both hands blazing with amber gold light, his entire body transformed into a living weapon of temporal fury. He wasn’t fighting a man anymore; he was trying to murder a concept.
Rex didn’t retreat. He didn’t dodge.
[Martial Arts Mastery] took control. As Theo’s first strike screamed toward his skull, Rex’s hand shot upward.
There was no wasted motion, no hesitation. His fingers closed around Theo’s wrist with the crushing precision of a hydraulic vice.
The sound of Theo’s bones groaning under the sudden pressure echoed off the silent buildings.
Rex didn’t just stop the blow; he seized the momentum.
With a fluid, violent twist of his hips, Rex pivoted. He used Theo’s own desperate, overextended force against him, converting the boy’s divine acceleration into a devastating leverage point.
"Too much force," Rex whispered.
In the microsecond before Theo’s body could react, Rex’s free hand slammed into the ground. [Earthen Authority] responded instantly to Rex’s command.
The cobblestones erupted, stone grinding against stone as the earth itself rose to meet the threat. A wall of hypercompressed granite shot upward from the street’s substrate.
Theo’s own momentum, redirected by Rex’s grip, carried him past Rex’s shoulder and directly into the rising monolith.
CRACK.
The sound of Theo’s ribs shattering against the stone wall was wet and sickening, followed immediately by the dull thud of his body collapsing against the unforgiving mass.

Theo didn’t fall. He didn’t even stagger. The recovery enhancement of the temporal designation is a backup feature that quickly brings a vessel back to the correct time after it has been used forcefully.
His body jerked away from the stone wall with a supernatural spring, his bones snapping back into place with audible clicks.
Before Rex could even finish processing the speed of that recovery, Theo was already airborne again, a golden blur of renewed fury.
’Second contact: Physical enhancement.’
Rex’s mind catalogued the incoming threat. The [Full Potential Adaptation] roared to life, weaving a protective lattice of reinforced cellular density around Rex’s organs and bones.
The blow landed a thunderous crack that would have liquefied a normal man’s ribcage, but Rex simply absorbed the shockwave, his body vibrating like a struck tuning fork.
’Third contact: Temporal acceleration.’
This was different. Theo wasn’t just moving fast; he was forcing his own personal timeline to accelerate, creating a localized pocket of hyper speed.
He was moving faster than the universe around him was permitted to move.
Rex made a conscious, calculated decision. He didn’t dodge and he didn’t counter.

He stood his ground and allowed the third contact with the temporal acceleration to wash over him. He needed to feel the exact interface where Theo’s accelerated timeline scraped against the world’s standard rate.
He needed the raw data on the friction.
’There.’
Rex felt it: a nauseating, reality-warping shear. For a fraction of a second, his body felt like it was being pulled apart by two different speeds of existence.
But the [Full Potential Adaptation] was faster. It didn’t just resist the acceleration; it seized it.
It mapped the frequency of Theo’s hyperspeed and integrated it into Rex’s own neurological pathways.
Before Theo’s accelerated strike could even complete its arc, Rex was already moving at Theo’s exact rate. The gap between them closed in a heartbeat.
Rex struck.
It wasn’t a flurry. It was a single, devastatingly precise application of force.
[Martial Arts Mastery] identified the exact anatomical weakness in Theo’s current posture: the vulnerable hinge where his accelerated momentum met his weakened center of gravity.
Because Rex had already integrated the physical enhancement parameters from the first two contacts, his fist carried the same divine weight as Theo’s own.
The impact sounded like a sledgehammer hitting a wet sack of concrete.
Theo’s body was launched backward. He flew through the air, a broken streak of gold, and slammed into the Earthen Authority construct Rex had raised earlier.
But the construct wasn’t passive. Rex commanded the stone to tighten, the earth itself lashing out with telekinetic force to pin Theo against the granite face.
Theo was trapped. His limbs were splayed, his chest pressed painfully against the cold stone, held there by a crushing pressure that made every breath a desperate struggle.
Blood leaked from his nose and mouth, dripping down his chin to stain the amber glow of his aura. His breathing was ragged, wet gasps that echoed off the silent walls of the district.
Through the haze of pain and the ringing in his ears, Theo lifted his head. His eyes, bloodshot and wild, found Rex’s.
Rex stood a few paces away, unruffled, the monster who had just dissected a god’s gift with clinical indifference. The silence between them was heavier than the stone pinning Theo to the wall.
"Where did you find Kaeleth?" Rex asked. His voice was quiet, almost conversational, which made the question feel like a death sentence.
Theo’s expression shuttered. The raw vulnerability of the moment retreated behind a wall of defensive numbness.
"He found me," he rasped, blood bubbling at the corner of his lips.
"At the cliff," Rex said.
A statement of fact. A confirmation of a pattern.
Theo’s face flickered. For the first time since the beginning of this nightmare, the flat, hollow emptiness cracked.
A flash of something—recognition, pain, perhaps even a sliver of shame—rippled across his features before he could suppress it.
"Yes," Theo whispered.
"He gave you the designation at the cliff," Rex said, his eyes narrowing as he read the confirmation written in the boy’s dilated pupils.
"Yes," Theo said.
