For a heartbeat, the hollow void in his eyes flickered with something dangerously close to terror—the raw, primal recognition that the physics of his reality had just been rewritten without his permission.
"I read it," Rex said, stepping forward into the amber glow.
His voice was unnervingly calm, cutting through the oppressive silence of the frozen city like a scalpel.
"The divine signature."
"The specific harmonic frequency of the temporal domain’s authority invested in a mortal vessel...
I can see the way your soul bleeds gold."
Rex studied Theo with the flat, patient attention of a scholar examining a rare specimen.
There was no malice in his gaze, no righteous fury, only a terrifyingly detached curiosity.
"I have been waiting for Kaeleth to make this move since I became aware of his operation...
I simply did not predict he would choose you as his scalpel."
"Does it matter?" Theo spat.
The words were wet, choked by the grief that still sat like lead in his lungs.
"Does it matter who gave me the power to erase you?"
"Yes," Rex said, tilting his head.
"It matters significantly."
"Because you are not Kaeleth’s Apostle in the conventional sense."
"An Apostle is a chosen partner; an instrument is something owned, something used until it breaks."
"There is a fundamental difference in how the power responds to your will, and that difference is what will determine how this ends."
Theo didn’t answer with words.
His right hand rose again, but this time the energy wasn’t just a blunt force; it was a shimmering distortion in the air.
Through [Divine Perception], Rex saw the mechanism engage.
This wasn’t the absolute cessation of the Time Stop; this was something more insidious.

A temporal deceleration is a field designed to drag the target’s subjective experience through molasses, reducing their reaction time to near zero while leaving them conscious enough to feel every second of their own helplessness.
The working struck Rex like an invisible wave of viscous liquid.
For seven tenths of a second, Rex’s world turned to sludge.
He felt his own synapses fire with agonizing slowness, his limbs feeling as though they were encased in cooling concrete.
His heart beat once, a thunderous, delayed sound that seemed to take an eternity to complete.
But in that same span, [Full Potential Adaptation] was screaming through his nervous system.
It seized the temporal distortion, dissected its mathematical framework, and rewrote Rex’s cellular resistance in real time.
By the eighth tenth of a second, the sludge evaporated.
Rex’s movement snapped back to full velocity as if the universe had suddenly remembered he existed.
Rex looked at Theo.
The boy stood frozen mid-gesture, his face twisted in a mask of horrified confusion.
He had thrown what should have been an inescapable prison, only to watch Rex walk through it as if it were nothing more than morning mist.
"The Time Stop worked on the first contact," Rex said, his voice carrying across the cobblestones with deadly clarity.
"The Slow worked on the first contact."
"The mathematical certainty of your designation means that everything you possess will work perfectly exactly once."
Rex’s eyes darkened, locking onto Theo’s with the inevitability of a guillotine blade.
"You have one of each...
And you’ve already spent them."
"AAAAAAAGGHH!"
The scream that tore from Theo’s throat wasn’t a battle cry.
It was a sound of pure, unadulterated psychological collapse.
It was the sound of a dam breaking the uncontrolled release of three years of grief, loss, and humiliation that had been held at bay by nothing but sheer, brittle willpower.
The dam had failed, and the flood was consuming him.
Theo lunged.
He abandoned all technique, all finesse, and all restraint.
He came at Rex with both hands blazing with amber gold light, his entire body transformed into a living weapon of temporal fury.
He wasn’t fighting a man anymore; he was trying to murder a concept.
Rex didn’t retreat.
He didn’t dodge.
[Martial Arts Mastery] took control.
As Theo’s first strike screamed toward his skull, Rex’s hand shot upward.
There was no wasted motion, no hesitation.
His fingers closed around Theo’s wrist with the crushing precision of a hydraulic vice.
The sound of Theo’s bones groaning under the sudden pressure echoed off the silent buildings.
Rex didn’t just stop the blow; he seized the momentum.
With a fluid, violent twist of his hips, Rex pivoted.
He used Theo’s own desperate, overextended force against him, converting the boy’s divine acceleration into a devastating leverage point.
"Too much force," Rex whispered.
In the microsecond before Theo’s body could react, Rex’s free hand slammed into the ground.
[Earthen Authority] responded instantly to Rex’s command.
The cobblestones erupted, stone grinding against stone as the earth itself rose to meet the threat.
A wall of hypercompressed granite shot upward from the street’s substrate.
Theo’s own momentum, redirected by Rex’s grip, carried him past Rex’s shoulder and directly into the rising monolith.
CRACK.
The sound of Theo’s ribs shattering against the stone wall was wet and sickening, followed immediately by the dull thud of his body collapsing against the unforgiving mass.
Theo didn’t fall.
He didn’t even stagger.
The recovery enhancement of the temporal designation is a backup feature that quickly brings a vessel back to the correct time after it has been used forcefully.
His body jerked away from the stone wall with a supernatural spring, his bones snapping back into place with audible clicks.
Before Rex could even finish processing the speed of that recovery, Theo was already airborne again, a golden blur of renewed fury.
’Second contact: Physical enhancement.’
Rex’s mind catalogued the incoming threat.
The [Full Potential Adaptation] roared to life, weaving a protective lattice of reinforced cellular density around Rex’s organs and bones.
The blow landed a thunderous crack that would have liquefied a normal man’s ribcage, but Rex simply absorbed the shockwave, his body vibrating like a struck tuning fork.
’Third contact: Temporal acceleration.’
This was different.
Theo wasn’t just moving fast; he was forcing his own personal timeline to accelerate, creating a localized pocket of hyper speed.
He was moving faster than the universe around him was permitted to move.
Rex made a conscious, calculated decision.
He didn’t dodge and he didn’t counter.
He stood his ground and allowed the third contact with the temporal acceleration to wash over him.
He needed to feel the exact interface where Theo’s accelerated timeline scraped against the world’s standard rate.
He needed the raw data on the friction.
’There.’
Rex felt it: a nauseating, reality-warping shear.
For a fraction of a second, his body felt like it was being pulled apart by two different speeds of existence.
But the [Full Potential Adaptation] was faster.
It didn’t just resist the acceleration; it seized it.
It mapped the frequency of Theo’s hyperspeed and integrated it into Rex’s own neurological pathways.
Before Theo’s accelerated strike could even complete its arc, Rex was already moving at Theo’s exact rate.
The gap between them closed in a heartbeat.
Rex struck.
It wasn’t a flurry.
It was a single, devastatingly precise application of force.
[Martial Arts Mastery] identified the exact anatomical weakness in Theo’s current posture: the vulnerable hinge where his accelerated momentum met his weakened center of gravity.
Because Rex had already integrated the physical enhancement parameters from the first two contacts, his fist carried the same divine weight as Theo’s own.
The impact sounded like a sledgehammer hitting a wet sack of concrete.
Theo’s body was launched backward.
He flew through the air, a broken streak of gold, and slammed into the Earthen Authority construct Rex had raised earlier.

Rex commanded the stone to tighten, the earth itself lashing out with telekinetic force to pin Theo against the granite face.
Theo was trapped.

"Yes," Theo said.

chapters.title: Chapter 1043. So, Funny Story About That Wall...
paragraphs: Rex stood motionless before the stone monolith, his silhouette cutting a sharp, unforgiving line against the amber haze of the frozen city. His mind was not on the pain in his jaw or the blood coating his knuckles; it was deep within the architecture of the moment.
Through [Divine Perception], he was reading the residual echoes of Theo’s soul the way the temporal designation hadn’t just been given but had been grafted onto a wound.
He connected the dots. The investment pattern of the divine authority, the specific harmonic frequency of the power, and the raw, desperate state of the vessel it inhabited.
All roads led to one location.
"You went there to jump," Rex said.
His voice wasn’t accusatory; it was the terrifyingly calm observation of a predator who had just discovered why the prey was so eager to die.
Theo’s jaw set with enough force that Rex could hear the grinding of bone against bone. His teeth clenched so hard the muscles in his neck stood out like steel cables.
He didn’t deny it. He couldn’t.
The truth was written in the way his aura flickered, not with divine pride, but with the exhausted residue of someone who had sought oblivion and found only a different kind of torment.
Rex studied him for several long seconds, measuring the boy’s breaking point.
Then, with a flick of his fingers, he released the telekinetic hold.

The Earthen Authority construct relaxed its grip, but Theo didn’t fall forward. He remained pressed against the stone, not out of defiance, but because his body had reached its absolute physiological limit.

The temporal designation’s recovery enhancement was working overtime, forcing his muscles to knit and his blood to flow, but it couldn’t mask the profound, bone-deep fatigue of someone who had burned their entire life force in a few desperate minutes.
Slowly, agonizingly, Theo slid down the face of the granite wall. His boots scraped against the stone before he collapsed into a seated position at its base, his head hanging low.
He lifted his hands, staring at them as if they belonged to a stranger. His fingers trembled with the aftershocks of the divine energy.

A thick stream of crimson blood traced a path from his brow, where the impact with the wall had split the skin down across his cheekbone, and dripped steadily onto his lap. The wound was fresh, angry, and pulsing with each ragged breath he took.
Rex stepped closer, looming over him like a monument to inevitable consequence. He said nothing.
Silence was more oppressive than any threat he could have hurled.
The atmosphere began to shift. The unnatural stillness of the city started to fray at the edges.
The golden glow of the temporal stop was losing its coherence, its radius contracting as Theo’s reserves drained into nothingness. The divine authority was exhausted, its grip on reality slipping.
Above them, the Nightwing household’s outer wall stood as a testament to the violence that had unfolded in the silence.
The original jagged wound from Rex’s initial impact remained stark against the masonry, now joined by a web of secondary fractures where Theo’s momentum had been redirected into the stone.
Then, the snap happened.
Time didn’t flow back in; it simply reasserted itself. There was no gradual acceleration, no warning.
One moment there was a vacuum of existence, and the next, reality rushed back in with the deafening violence of a dam breaking.
The pigeons mid-flight suddenly completed their arc with a flurry of wings. The fountain’s water, suspended in crystal midair, crashed into its basin with a sudden, chaotic splash.
In the northern district, the distant sounds of construction equipment hummed back to life as if they had never stopped.
But the most immediate sound came from above.
The structural damage to the Nightwing manor finally registered with the physics of the real world.

The weakened masonry groaned, the ancient wood settled with a series of sharp, pistol-like cracks, and from inside the house, the startled shouts of inhabitants erupted alarms beginning to wail as the household realized their fortress had been violated while they slept.

From two hundred meters away, toward the direction of the Academy, a different kind of violence registered. Through the passive geological read of his [Earthen Authority], Rex felt it before he heard it: a seismic shudder traveling through the city’s foundation.

It was the specific, bone-deep vibration of a massive object his own body slamming into stone. The data stream in his mind painted a clear picture: the academy’s outer teaching hall had taken a direct hit, its structural integrity compromised at the exact coordinates where he had been hurled during the earlier escalation.
The city didn’t wake up gently. It tore itself awake.

The silence of the temporal freeze was replaced by a cacophony of normalcy that felt violently wrong: the grinding of gears, distant car alarms, the chatter of morning pedestrians, and the low hum of a world that had forgotten it was supposed to be frozen.
But beneath that veneer of normalcy lay the unmistakable tension of a city that had just been struck by an invisible hammer.
People were stopping in their tracks, heads turning toward the damage, eyes widening at the fractured masonry and the unnatural stillness that still clung to the air like smoke.
Approximately forty-five seconds after reality reasserted itself, the Academy’s outer gates burst open.
Valentina emerged. She didn’t run, which implied panic, and Valentina was beyond panic.
She moved with a terrifying, deliberate speed, each stride measured and lethal, the gait of a predator who had already processed the variables and was now moving to neutralize the threat.

Close behind her came Morwenna. Rex’s mind briefly catalogued the error in his tactical assessment: he hadn’t predicted Morwenna would be the immediate second responder, but as his [Divine Perception] analyzed the scene, the logic became undeniable.
The Nightwing household’s outer wall was shattered; the damage was visible even from the Academy’s gates. It was impossible for her to ignore.
The two women skidded to a halt at the edge of the street, their eyes scanning the wreckage with deadly precision.
Their gaze first locked onto Rex. He stood twenty meters from the Nightwing wall, his breathing steady despite the carnage.

His jacket was displaced, hanging crookedly from the shoulder where the initial impact had nearly torn it free, and his knuckles were stained dark with dried blood. He looked less like a student and more like the epicenter of a disaster.
Then, their eyes shifted to the Academy building. The outer teaching hall bore the ugly, indented scar of Rex’s impact, a crater in the stone that spoke of inhuman force.
Finally, their eyes traveled upward, following the line of the crumbling Nightwing wall to the base of the Earthen construct.

There, slumped against the stone like a broken marionette, was Theo. His face was a mask of blood and exhaustion, his golden aura flickering like a dying candle, his eyes hollowed out by the weight of what he had just discovered about himself.
The three of them stood frozen in a triangle of unspoken violence: the hunter, the witnesses, and the broken instrument.

chapters.title: Chapter 1044. He Told His Grandmother to Shut Up, I Just Lay Down
paragraphs: Theo hadn’t remained broken. As reality rushed back in, the temporal designation’s recovery enhancement had kicked into a desperate, automated overdrive.
It didn’t heal him; it simply forcibly reanimated his systems, stitching together failing nerve clusters and forcing blood through depleted veins just enough to grant him basic mobility.
He had dragged himself up from the base of the construct, his movements jerky and unnatural, like a marionette being pulled by invisible, cruel strings.

Now, he hovered approximately thirty meters above the street. He possessed no wings, no true flight; he was simply suspended there by the residual temporal enhancement, the designation anchoring his personal timeline to a fixed point in space to prevent him from plummeting to his death.
He looked like a fallen angel bleeding out in midair.

His right hand was pressed against his skull as if trying to hold his thoughts inside his head. His left hand covered his right eye, fingers splayed to catch the crimson stream flowing from the gash above his brow.
The blood was warm and thick, tracing a wet, grotesque path down his cheek, dripping off his chin in rhythmic splatters that seemed to echo in the sudden silence of the street.
He was breathing. But it wasn’t the breath of a living boy; it was the wet, rattling gasp of a survivor who had fought his way through hell only to find nothing waiting for him on the other side.
Each inhale was a struggle, each exhale a shudder that rocked his entire frame.
"Theo."
Morwenna’s voice cut through the ambient noise of the awakening city. It wasn’t the voice of the Nightwing matriarch, the cold, untouchable authority that commanded respect and fear.
This was something else. It was a voice stripped of formality, ancient and raw, carrying the weight of decades of shared history.
It was the register reserved for those who had seen the child before they saw the weapon.
"Theo," she said again, her voice cracking with a vulnerability that seemed almost painful to witness. "What have you done?"

The question hung between them, more devastating than any physical blow Rex had landed. It wasn’t just a question about the broken walls or the cratered Academy building; it was a question about his soul.
Theo looked down at her. His gaze was unfocused, glassy with pain and something far more dangerous: resignation.

In that moment, his entire identity—the anger, the power, the desperate need to prove himself—collapsed. He had entered this confrontation in a state of absolute nihilism, believing that he had nothing left to lose.
But he had been mistaken. He discovered, with the brutal clarity of a blade to the throat, that he did have something to lose: the memory of the woman looking up at him.
He had lost the one tether that connected him to his own humanity.
He squeezed his right eye shut against the blood, the motion sending fresh crimson streaming through his fingers. He couldn’t look at her.
He couldn’t bear to see his own failure reflected in the eyes of the only person who remembered who he used to be.
He said nothing. The silence that followed was absolute, broken only by the wet, irregular sound of his failing breath.
"Theo."

Morwenna’s voice shifted. The vulnerability that had momentarily cracked her composure vanished, replaced instantly by something far more dangerous: the razor-edged sharpness of a matriarch whose fear had curdled into rage.
It was the register of a woman who used anger as armor, a familiar, practiced weapon she wielded whenever the world threatened to unravel beneath her feet.
"Answer me!" she demanded, each word striking like a whipcrack. "What did you do?!"
"Why is the Academy’s teaching hall cratered?!"
"Why is the Nightwing wall shattered like it was struck by siege engines?!"
"And what in God’s name are those marks on your skin?" She gestured violently toward the raw, bleeding lacerations and the unnatural pallor of his exhaustion. "Look at me, Theo!"
Theo didn’t look at her. Not at first.

His gaze drifted upward, staring into the empty blue of the morning sky as if searching for a crack in reality where he might slip through and disappear. When his eyes finally descended to meet Morwenna’s, they were cold.
Dead.
"Shut up."
The words didn’t just carry sound; they carried consequences. They landed in the center of the street with the devastating weight of a sacrilege.

For three heartbeats, the entire world seemed to hold its breath. The pedestrians, the construction crews, and Valentina and Morwenna—everyone present— froze, processing the impossible: Theo Morr Nightwing had just spoken to Morwenna Nightwing with the casual venom of a stranger.
The hierarchy of the household hadn’t just been challenged; it had been incinerated.

Rex watched the tableau unfold with detached, analytical precision. His [Divine Perception] mapped the micro expressions spreading across Morwenna’s face: the flash of genuine shock, the whitening of her knuckles, and the way her pupils dilated as her fury mounted.

He looked up at Theo, suspended thirty meters above them, a broken god bleeding out against a backdrop of divine failure. The temporal designation was sputtering now, its energy depleted, barely maintaining the boy’s altitude and forcing his body through a grotesque, automated healing process that looked more like torture than recovery.
Rex felt the adrenaline fading, leaving behind a bone-deep ache and the strange, hollow calm that follows a catastrophe. He decided he had done enough standing for one day.

With deliberate, unhurried movements, Rex lowered himself to the asphalt. He lay down on his back in the middle of the street, staring straight up at the clouds, as if the carnage behind him was nothing more than background noise.
"Good morning," he said.
His voice was flat, eerily even the tone of a man who had just survived a hurricane and decided that the best course of action was to take a nap.
Valentina’s head snapped toward him, her eyes narrowing with lethal suspicion. Morwenna’s fury momentarily wavered as she turned to glare at the boy lying insolently on the ground.
Rex didn’t blink. He kept his eyes fixed on the sky.
"Someone with a new Apostle designation arrived approximately seven minutes ago," he stated, narrating the event like a clinical report.

"They attempted to address certain... specific concerns they had regarding my continued existence." He paused, letting the implication of the near-death struggle hang in the air. "The attempt was not successful."
"The individual in question is currently hovering directly above us."
He shifted his head slightly, looking at Valentina and Morwenna from his horizontal position on the pavement, his expression one of mild, almost bored amusement.
"If I were you," Rex added, his voice carrying a note of genuine warning beneath the nonchalance, "you might want to start a conversation with him that doesn’t involve him telling you to shut up."
"He isn’t exactly in the right state of mind for pleasantries."

His gaze was unfocused, glassy with pain and something far more dangerous: resignation.
In that moment, his entire identity—the anger, the power, the desperate need to prove himself—collapsed.
He had entered this confrontation in a state of absolute nihilism, believing that he had nothing left to lose.
But he had been mistaken.
He discovered, with the brutal clarity of a blade to the throat, that he did have something to lose: the memory of the woman looking up at him.
He had lost the one tether that connected him to his own humanity.
He squeezed his right eye shut against the blood, the motion sending fresh crimson streaming through his fingers.
He couldn’t look at her.
He couldn’t bear to see his own failure reflected in the eyes of the only person who remembered who he used to be.
He said nothing.
The silence that followed was absolute, broken only by the wet, irregular sound of his failing breath.
"Theo."
Morwenna’s voice shifted.
The vulnerability that had momentarily cracked her composure vanished, replaced instantly by something far more dangerous: the razor-edged sharpness of a matriarch whose fear had curdled into rage.
It was the register of a woman who used anger as armor, a familiar, practiced weapon she wielded whenever the world threatened to unravel beneath her feet.
"Answer me!" she demanded, each word striking like a whipcrack.
"What did you do?!"
"Why is the Academy’s teaching hall cratered?!"
"Why is the Nightwing wall shattered like it was struck by siege engines?!"
"And what in God’s name are those marks on your skin?" She gestured violently toward the raw, bleeding lacerations and the unnatural pallor of his exhaustion.
"Look at me, Theo!"
Theo didn’t look at her.
Not at first.
His gaze drifted upward, staring into the empty blue of the morning sky as if searching for a crack in reality where he might slip through and disappear.
When his eyes finally descended to meet Morwenna’s, they were cold.
Dead.
"Shut up."
The words didn’t just carry sound; they carried consequences.
They landed in the center of the street with the devastating weight of a sacrilege.
For three heartbeats, the entire world seemed to hold its breath.

The pedestrians, the construction crews, and Valentina and Morwenna—everyone present— froze, processing the impossible: Theo Morr Nightwing had just spoken to Morwenna Nightwing with the casual venom of a stranger.
The hierarchy of the household hadn’t just been challenged; it had been incinerated.
Rex watched the tableau unfold with detached, analytical precision.
His [Divine Perception] mapped the micro expressions spreading across Morwenna’s face: the flash of genuine shock, the whitening of her knuckles, and the way her pupils dilated as her fury mounted.
He looked up at Theo, suspended thirty meters above them, a broken god bleeding out against a backdrop of divine failure.

The temporal designation was sputtering now, its energy depleted, barely maintaining the boy’s altitude and forcing his body through a grotesque, automated healing process that looked more like torture than recovery.
Rex felt the adrenaline fading, leaving behind a bone-deep ache and the strange, hollow calm that follows a catastrophe.
He decided he had done enough standing for one day.
With deliberate, unhurried movements, Rex lowered himself to the asphalt.
He lay down on his back in the middle of the street, staring straight up at the clouds, as if the carnage behind him was nothing more than background noise.
"Good morning," he said.
His voice was flat, eerily even the tone of a man who had just survived a hurricane and decided that the best course of action was to take a nap.
Valentina’s head snapped toward him, her eyes narrowing with lethal suspicion.
Morwenna’s fury momentarily wavered as she turned to glare at the boy lying insolently on the ground.
Rex didn’t blink.
He kept his eyes fixed on the sky.
"Someone with a new Apostle designation arrived approximately seven minutes ago," he stated, narrating the event like a clinical report.
"They attempted to address certain... specific concerns they had regarding my continued existence." He paused, letting the implication of the near-death struggle hang in the air.
"The attempt was not successful."
"The individual in question is currently hovering directly above us."
He shifted his head slightly, looking at Valentina and Morwenna from his horizontal position on the pavement, his expression one of mild, almost bored amusement.
"If I were you," Rex added, his voice carrying a note of genuine warning beneath the nonchalance, "you might want to start a conversation with him that doesn’t involve him telling you to shut up."
"He isn’t exactly in the right state of mind for pleasantries."

chapters.title: Chapter 1045. The Distance She Never Spoke Across Before
paragraphs: Morwenna had spoken to Theo across many distances in her life, each gulf defined by the shifting architecture of their shared history.
There was the intimate distance of childhood, the physical span that required her to crouch, bringing her eye level to his, offering a sanctuary of shared breath.
Then there was the growing chasm of adolescence: the distance between two bodies occupying the same house but inhabiting separate, warring territories of self.
Eventually, that grew into the sterile, political distance of a household head addressing a chosen heir, a formal, measured space where every word was weighed for its impact on legacy.

She had navigated the spaces of grief, the heights of celebration, and that treacherous, careful neutrality required when speaking truth to a young person who would inevitably recoil if the medicine tasted too bitter.
But she had never spoken to him across this distance.
Forty meters of yawning, impossible void separated them. Theo did not stand; he hovered, suspended in the amber gold residue of a temporal designation gone catastrophically wrong.

The air around him screamed with the violence of its own existence. It was a disturbed, hemorrhaging atmosphere, bucking and convulsing as it was forced to sustain two conflicting temporal states simultaneously.
The very fabric of reality seemed to fray at his edges, sparking with lethal, chronological static.
"Theo," she said.
Her voice cut through the howling distortion, carrying the precise register she had used when he was a child, the tone that bypassed anger to deliver the cold, unvarnished weight of consequence.
Not punishment, but reality.
Theo turned.

His eyes were no longer the eyes of the boy she had raised; they were twin craters of molten hatred, burning with an insanity that transcended mere rage. His jaw was set in a grotesque snarl, muscles twitching with a manic energy that seemed to threaten tearing his own skin apart.
Inside his mind, there was no longer any room for memory, only the rhythmic, pounding crescendo of vengeance.
’Break it,’ something primal and shattered whispered behind his ribs. ’Break the world that made you.’
’Break her. Break everything until there is nothing left to hurt.’
"You think you can still speak to me like that?" His voice was a fractured ruin, wet with the copper tang of blood that leaked from his split lips. "Like I’m still your precious heir?"
"Like I’m still something you can shape with your pretty little lessons?"

A vein throbbed violently in his temple, nearly bursting beneath the strain of his transformation. The golden energy around him surged, a shockwave of temporal displacement that cracked the ground beneath Morwenna’s feet.
The sound was like bone grinding against stone, a wet, splintering noise that echoed in the hollow of her chest.

"I am the consequence you never prepared for, Morwenna," he spat, his fingers curling into claws as the energy began to calcify around his knuckles like armor made of dying seconds. "I am the reality that eats its own creator."
He looked at her.

Blood continued its slow, obscene journey down Theo’s face. The gash across his brow was deep, a jagged wound that wept crimson steadily enough to coat his jawline and drip onto his collar in hot, rhythmic splatters.
His right eye was squeezed half shut to shield it from the stinging salt of his own blood, but his left eye remained fixed on Morwenna wide, unblinking, and terrifyingly analytical.
It was the gaze of a predator weighing whether the prey before him was worth the effort of the kill.
"You can come down," Morwenna said, her voice steady despite the temporal static tearing at the air around her.
"No," he said.
The word was clipped, vibrating with the unstable energy coursing through his veins.
"Then I can come up."
It wasn’t a threat. It was the flat, terrifyingly calm statement of someone who had already accepted the cost of the ascent.
"Don’t," Theo warned.
His fingers flexed, and the sound of tendons snapping under the strain of his power echoed like breaking twigs.
’Stay back,’ his mind screamed, even as his body prepared to launch. ’If you come closer, I will have to destroy you too.’
’I will have to tear the sky apart to keep you from seeing what I’ve become.’
"Theo," Morwenna said, stepping forward despite the way the ground groaned beneath her. "I have known you since you were three years old."
"I have watched every fracture in your character, every moment of growth... I know what this madness looks like from inside its storm, and I know what it looks like from the safety of the shore."
"I am asking you; I am begging you to let me tell you what I see from the outside before you decide that the darkness inside you is the only truth that exists."
Theo’s jaw worked silently. His teeth ground together with a wet, audible creak.
He wasn’t dismissing her; he was processing her words like venom, deciding whether they were a cure or simply another lie to be purged.
"What happened to you," Morwenna asked, her voice cracking slightly with the first sign of emotion, "in this last month?"
"I need to understand. I need to know the shape of this pain."
"You were there for most of it," Theo snapped.
The temporal distortion around him flared brighter, casting jagged, dancing shadows across his blood-streaked face.
"I was present for what was visible," she countered, refusing to flinch as a shard of debris, flung by the temporal wind, whistled past her ear. "I am asking about what was hidden."
"What happened in the silence?"
He looked at her then, and for a heartbeat, the insanity wavered, revealing a hollow, aching void beneath.
"Everything," he whispered, the word carrying more weight than any scream. "Everything that was mine stopped being mine."
"Bit by bit. Piece by piece. Like someone walking through my life with a sledgehammer, systematically dismantling the walls until there’s nowhere left to stand."
"Rex," she said, naming the wound.
"Yes," he spat, the name tasting like bile. "Rex."
"And you believe," she said, stepping closer even as the golden energy began to sear the edges of her clothes, "that this... this slaughter, this unraveling of reality is the answer to that loss?"
"I believe," Theo said, and his voice shifted.
The flat, numb recitation of his losses ignited into something hot, volatile, and dangerously focused. "I believe there is nothing left to address, Morwenna."
"There is no ’fixing’ this. There is no rebuilding. The only variable left is the equation itself."
"He exists, and I exist. Those two facts are incompatible."
"One of us has to be erased to make the math work again."
"Theo, listen to me... Please."

"I have listened to you for twenty-two years more!" he roared, the sound tearing from his throat as a shockwave of golden light punched outward, cracking the stone floor between them. "I listened to the council, I listened to the tutors, I listened to the gods, and I listened to you!"

"I followed every rule, I bled for every lesson, I performed every duty with perfect precision, and the result is that I am standing here in the ruins of my life, and he is standing there, untouched, breathing, alive."
His chest heaved, his breath coming in ragged, wet gasps. "I did everything I was supposed to do, and none of it mattered!"
"NOTHING!"
"It mattered," she insisted, her eyes glistening with unshed tears. "Every sacrifice, every choice mattered."
"To whom?" he asked.

The question wasn’t angry anymore. It was worse. It was cold, clinical, and utterly devoid of hope. It was the question of a man who had spent his entire life tracking the consequences of his actions, only to find that the universe refused to keep score.

chapters.title: Chapter 1046. A Voice Coiled in the Background Like a Sleeping Serpent
paragraphs: Morwenna stared up at her great-grandson, suspended in that hemorrhaging amber sky forty meters above her.
She felt a hollow, sickening sensation in the pit of her stomach, the precise, cold dread that comes when one recognizes a situation that possesses no possible beneficial outcome.
There was no path here that ended in healing; there was only the choice between different flavors of catastrophe.
"To me," she said, her voice cracking like thin ice under the pressure of the temporal howling. "To Elaris... To the household."
"The household," Theo repeated.

The way he said it made the word sound foreign, like a relic from a dead civilization. His voice held the hollow inflection of someone who had watched a sacred concept be stripped of its meaning and replaced with something transactional and cruel.
"The household is currently being directed by the person I just tried to kill."
"You’re speaking of a ghost, Morwenna. A structure that burned down while you were still busy admiring the blueprints."
Morwenna froze. The silence that followed was worse than the temporal screaming.
She had no answer for that. The truth of his words struck her with the force of a physical blow, leaving her momentarily breathless.

That was the problem: the fundamental, unsolvable fracture between them. From approximately two seconds into this confrontation, she knew that this conversation would not be the salvation she had hoped for.
She wasn’t a teacher or a great-grandmother anymore; she was a witness to a massacre in progress.
But she could not stop. She would not let him slip into the abyss without one last fight.

"What you have received from the god who spoke to you to get this such power..." she cried out, stepping forward as the golden energy lashed at her skin, leaving stinging red welts across her cheekbones, "is not what you call true power, Theo!"
"Do you hear me?! It is not power! It is more than a leash!"
"And it is a direction carved into your soul by something that doesn’t understand what it means to bleed, to hurt, or to love."
"That direction was chosen for you, not by you! It was chosen based on what that entity thinks you can be used for—a weapon, a tool, a vessel—not based on who you actually are!"
Theo’s head tilted to the side. The movement was unnervingly smooth, almost mechanical.
Blood from his brow wound trickled into his left eye now, blurring his vision with a crimson haze, but his stare remained unnervingly sharp.
"That is very wise," he said, his tone dripping with a terrifying, mocking sweetness. "It is also exactly what Rex says.
"He says it to the council. He says it to the servants."
"He says it to everyone, about everything, with that same patronizing smile."
Morwenna felt a surge of fury beneath her grief. "You cannot win an argument against me simply by pointing out that your argument was made first by someone else!"
"I can," Theo snapped, his voice suddenly dropping to a guttural snarl that vibrated in Morwenna’s very bones.

The temporal field around him convulsed, sending a spray of molten amber shards downward that tore through the stone floor like shrapnel. "I can when the ’someone else’ is the reason the argument exists in the first place! Rex didn’t just give me a different perspective, Morwenna; he took everything until there was nothing left for me to argue about except his own damn existence!"
A manic grin split his bloody face, revealing teeth stained pink. Inside his mind, the darkness was screaming louder than the storm.
’She’s trying to cage you again,’ the voice hissed. ’She’s trying to put you back in the box.’
’Break the box. Break her. Break the world.’
Theo tore his gaze away from Morwenna, his eyes snapping toward Rex. Below, on the street level between Valentina and the Academy’s outer gate, Rex stood like a monument of unshakeable calm.
Something flickered across Theo’s face, a microscopic fracture in his madness, the involuntary expression of a man who has just been struck by a truth he desperately wants to deny.
Then, the voice arrived.

It wasn’t a scream or a thunderclap; it was the same cold, ancient presence that had haunted him since the cliff’s edge. It had been there, coiled in the background of his consciousness like a sleeping serpent, not intrusive enough to feel alien, but present enough to feel like part of his own shadow.
’Do not let her speak more.’ Kaeleth’s voice was devoid of drama.
It was the flat, surgical delivery of an entity that had been communicating through this channel long enough to know exactly how to twist the knife. ’She is already doing it, Theo.’
’She is already sowing the seeds of doubt.’
’Can you not hear it? Can you not hear the tremor in your own conviction?’
Theo looked back at Morwenna, his pupils dilating despite the blood streaming into his eye.
He could hear it. Kaeleth was right.

There was a foreign texture to his own voice, a crackle of uncertainty he recognized from twenty-nine years of playing political games he didn’t believe in. When he argued, he usually sounded like steel; now, he sounded like breaking glass.
’She will tell you more,’ Kaeleth whispered, the words sliding into his mind like oil. ’And more.’
’And by the end of it, you will have talked yourself into a corner so deep that you will never find the light again.’
’And when you try to back out, when you try to reclaim your fury, the cost will be higher than any blood you could spill today.’
’You will lose yourself entirely.’
Theo’s gaze shifted violently to Rex.

Rex was leaning in toward Valentina, speaking with the measured, hypnotic cadence of a predator who knew exactly how to make his prey agree with him. Theo watched as Valentina’s shoulders relaxed, her posture gradually aligning with Rex’s framing, her resistance melting away like wax near a flame.

Rex wasn’t even looking at him. He was calmly orchestrating a new reality while Theo hung suspended in the air, bleeding from a dozen wounds, and Morwenna offered him a lifeline of logic that he could feel, god help him, actually working.
The realization burned worse than the temporal energy searing his flesh. The rage boiled over, not as passion but as a cold, killing frost.
"You are doing it again," Theo said.
His voice had gone utterly flat, stripped of all inflection. It was the dead register of a man who had stopped considering options and had returned to his original, violent purpose.
"Theo—" Morwenna started, reaching out a hand as if she could physically grasp the fading pieces of his soul.
"You are on his side," Theo interrupted, each word landing like a hammer blow against an anvil. "Not consciously."
"I don’t think you even possess the self-awareness to realize you’ve betrayed me!"
"But he has been in this household for one month, Morwenna... One FUCKING month!"
The temporal field around him bucked violently, a shockwave of gold energy sending debris cascading down like lethal rain. Theo’s breathing was wet and labored, but his words were precise.
"You have been present for every atrocity this month has produced."

"You have watched the foundations crack. And yet, the way you are talking to me right now, the register you’re using, the way you’re carefully curating your points, the way you’re waiting for me to explain myself like some wayward child—it’s not concern!"
"It’s judgment." His teeth bared in a bloody snarl. "You’re talking to me like someone who has already decided what my explanation means!"
"You’ve already written my verdict, haven’t you?"

’You will lose yourself entirely.’
Theo’s gaze shifted violently to Rex.
Rex was leaning in toward Valentina, speaking with the measured, hypnotic cadence of a predator who knew exactly how to make his prey agree with him.
Theo watched as Valentina’s shoulders relaxed, her posture gradually aligning with Rex’s framing, her resistance melting away like wax near a flame.
Rex wasn’t even looking at him.

He was calmly orchestrating a new reality while Theo hung suspended in the air, bleeding from a dozen wounds, and Morwenna offered him a lifeline of logic that he could feel, god help him, actually working.
The realization burned worse than the temporal energy searing his flesh.
The rage boiled over, not as passion but as a cold, killing frost.
"You are doing it again," Theo said.
His voice had gone utterly flat, stripped of all inflection.
It was the dead register of a man who had stopped considering options and had returned to his original, violent purpose.
"Theo—" Morwenna started, reaching out a hand as if she could physically grasp the fading pieces of his soul.
"You are on his side," Theo interrupted, each word landing like a hammer blow against an anvil.
"Not consciously."
"I don’t think you even possess the self-awareness to realize you’ve betrayed me!"
"But he has been in this household for one month, Morwenna...
One FUCKING month!"
The temporal field around him bucked violently, a shockwave of gold energy sending debris cascading down like lethal rain.
Theo’s breathing was wet and labored, but his words were precise.
"You have been present for every atrocity this month has produced."
"You have watched the foundations crack.

And yet, the way you are talking to me right now, the register you’re using, the way you’re carefully curating your points, the way you’re waiting for me to explain myself like some wayward child—it’s not concern!"
"It’s judgment." His teeth bared in a bloody snarl.
"You’re talking to me like someone who has already decided what my explanation means!"
"You’ve already written my verdict, haven’t you?"

chapters.title: Chapter 1047. A Wind That Blew From Yesterday and Tomorrow
paragraphs: Morwenna remained silent, her face pale beneath the flickering amber light. The silence stretched between them, taut as a bowstring ready to snap, filled only by the wet, ragged rasp of Theo’s breathing and the distant thunder of temporal distortions.
"I am not on his side," she finally whispered, though the words lacked the conviction Theo needed to hear.
"Then fucking prove it to me!" Theo screamed.
The outburst was primal, a raw eruption of agony that tore through his throat. Blood sprayed from his lips as he roared.
"Prove it, Morwenna! Tell me that what happened to me this fucking month was wrong!"

"Tell me that what that bastard did to this goddamn family was wrong! Say it! Say it without qualifying it, without adding ’but,’ without adding ’if,’ without those fucking pathetic excuses you use to soften the blow!"
He leaned forward in the air, the gravitational distortion around him making his body jerk like a marionette on broken strings. "Say it plainly, or shut your fucking mouth and get out of my way!"
Morwenna closed her eyes. For three agonizing seconds, she said nothing.
Theo watched her. He watched the way her eyelids trembled, the way her jaw tightened.
In that silence, he heard every unspoken word, every hesitation, and every unspoken concession to the new reality Rex had imposed.
"I thought so," Theo said, his voice dropping to a deadly, venomous whisper. "You can’t even say it."
"You’re too fucking terrified of being wrong about him."
"What happened to your position in this household," she began, her voice carefully measured, armored in that academic detachment he now loathed, "was the result of your own choices as much as—"
"FUCK YOU! DONE!" Theo shrieked.
The temporal energy around him detonated in a burst of golden shrapnel. A chunk of stone from the Academy wall tore past Morwenna’s head, missing her by inches.
"I’m done listening to your fucking lies disguised as wisdom!"
His head snapped toward the street level. His neck tendons stood out like cables.
Down there, Rex was still moving, still weaving his web. He was finishing something.

Theo could see it in the way Valentina leaned forward, the way her eyes followed Rex’s lips; she wasn’t just listening anymore; she was being consumed. The conversation had moved past debate; they were approaching the inevitable conclusion of Rex’s design.
Theo’s gaze locked onto Rex. His vision was swimming in crimson; his ribs felt like they were grinding together with every breath, but his hatred was the only thing keeping him upright in the air.
Rex, as if sensing the exact moment his puppet’s strings were being cut, slowly lifted his head. He glanced up, meeting Theo’s bloodshot, murderous stare with a terrifying, placid calm.

Rex looked like a man observing weather patterns: patient, detached, and utterly in control of the storm. He looked like a man who had already calculated every variable of this slaughter and found them all wanting.
Rex murmured something final to Valentina, a gentle hand perhaps touching her shoulder, before he fully turned his attention to the monster hovering above.

He looked up at Theo with the expression of someone who had been studying a problem from thirty meters below and had finally seen the entire, ugly picture. His eyes were cold, empty of malice but full of a devastating certainty.
"The same attacks," Rex said, his voice carrying upward through the chaos with unnatural clarity, "will not produce different outcomes, Theo. "
"You already know this... You’re just repeating a failed script."
Theo’s fingers curled into fists so tight his knuckles cracked audibly.
"I know," he spat, a glob of bloody phlegm falling from his chin. "And I’m not planning on using the same fucking attacks."
Rex’s lips curled into the faintest, most predatory shadow of a smile.
"Good," Rex said. "Neither am I."

Theo’s expression fractured. It wasn’t just anger anymore; it was something far more volatile, a twisted amalgam of grief, betrayal, and a psychotic break that severed his last remaining ties to sanity.
His eyes rolled back slightly, revealing bloodshot whites, before snapping forward with a focus that was utterly inhuman.
Rex watched that transformation with the detached fascination of a scientist observing a volatile chemical reaction.
He didn’t flinch, and he didn’t even brace. He simply waited for the inevitable detonation.
The conclusion arrived not as words but as a scream.
It was not the calculated, righteous fury Theo had displayed earlier. That had been a performance, a rehearsed list of grievances.

This was something far more primal. This was the sound of a man whose psyche had been shredded into confetti, a raw, unorganized shriek that tore through his vocal cords until blood sprayed from his mouth in crimson droplets.
It was the sound of someone who had passed beyond the ability to describe his pain and had become the pain itself.
Then, the dam broke.

Every ounce of the temporal designation’s available output erupted from Theo’s position in a catastrophic omnidirectional blast. The amber gold aura, which had previously maintained a soft, controlled glow, suddenly intensified into a blinding, malevolent sun.
It wasn’t a targeted attack; it wasn’t a surgical strike. This was a tantrum of cosmic proportions, the raw, unfiltered authority of the temporal domain asserting itself over reality.
Time did not stop. It shattered.

The distortion field tore through the air like jagged glass, and the world began to scream along with Theo. The buildings surrounding the Nightwing household and the Academy’s outer walls began to hemorrhage their own history.

Stone surfaces flickered violently between states of existence: ancient, crumbling ruins that had stood centuries ago bled through the modern masonry; cracks from Rex’s earlier impacts would spider across the walls, vanish as the stone regressed to its pristine state, and then reappear with renewed violence as the timeline stuttered.
The very fabric of spacetime was being flayed alive.

Morwenna collapsed to her knees, a strangled gasp escaping her lips. The distortion’s effect on biological systems was horrific; it wasn’t a direct assault on her flesh but a byproduct of her cells trying to exist in multiple moments at once.

Her body was fighting a losing war against its own continuity. Her heart attempted to beat in three different seconds simultaneously; her lungs struggled to draw breath from air that was both present and thirty years gone.
The sheer metabolic cost of maintaining a singular biological existence against the temporal flicker was draining her reserves at a suicidal rate.
"Gods above—" Valentina’s voice was swallowed by the temporal howling.
Her training took over before her conscious mind could even process the threat. As the headmaster of the Grand Academy, her reflexes were forged in centuries of magical warfare.

Without hesitation, she raised her hands, weaving a complex temporal stabilization field, a magical anchor designed to insist upon a single, consistent timeline within a defined radius. The shimmering barrier snapped into existence around her, creating a pocket of relative normalcy.

The five-meter radius of her protection included Rex. He stood beside her as the barrier solidified, his expression unchanged, his breathing steady even as the world around them dissolved into temporal chaos.
Then, Rex moved.

With a deliberate, almost casual step, Rex walked out of the protection of Valentina’s field. He stepped directly into the meat grinder of the distortion, leaving the safety of the stabilized timeline behind.
His cloak fluttered in a wind that blew from yesterday and tomorrow simultaneously, but his feet remained planted on the ground as if he owned the very concept of time itself.
He looked up at Theo, standing amidst the wreckage of reality, his eyes cold, patient, and utterly terrifying.

chapters.title: Chapter 1048. A Shadow That Refused to Disappear
paragraphs: "The area expression," Rex murmured.
His voice didn’t carry to Theo; it was a private cataloguing, a cold, clinical assessment delivered in the flat register of a predator analyzing the mechanics of a trap. "Broader range."
"Drastically reduced precision."
"The tradeoff is precisely what you’d expect from a power source operating at overload."
Rex didn’t hesitate. He didn’t seek cover.

He began to walk not away from the chaos, but directly into the eye of the storm. He marched toward the epicenter where the temporal distortion was most violent, where reality was being shredded into a thousand screaming fragments of past and future.

Inside his mind, the machinery of the Full Potential Adaptation roared to life. The first contact analysis surged through his consciousness like liquid mercury, scanning the mechanism of the distortion.

It registered the anomaly: this wasn’t the surgical precision of Theo’s previous temporal stops or the gradual drag of his temporal slows. This was a new category, an uncontrolled, omnidirectional area expression.
Because it was new, the adaptation’s protective coverage had not yet extended to it.
’First contact will deliver full effect,’ the system warned.
Rex felt it immediately. The distortion slammed into his biological system like a physical assault.
It wasn’t just pain; it was the nauseating horror of existential uncertainty. His timeline began to flicker.
For terrifying micro-moments, his bones felt like they were both ancient dust and unborn marrow. His blood felt as though it were flowing backward through his veins before surging forward again.

His consciousness stuttered, his mind grasping at a present moment that refused to stay solid. His flesh screamed as cells attempted to exist across multiple temporal states simultaneously, the sheer friction of time tearing at his molecular continuity.
The adaptation ran its analysis through the agony.
’Three point four seconds.’
For three and a half seconds, Rex existed in a state of quantum torment, his body pushed to the absolute brink of dissolution.

Then, with the silent click of a completed equation, the adaptation’s coverage snapped into place. The temporal distortions continued to howl around him, and the buildings continued to flicker and decay in the background, but the effect on Rex simply... stopped.
The distortion was still running at full power, but it was no longer touching him. He had become a foreign object in the timeline that the storm could not grasp.
Rex steadied his breathing, his eyes locking onto the broken figure above.
"That one took longer," Rex said, his voice cutting through the temporal static with terrifying calm. "New category."
Theo stared down at him, his face a mask of pure, unadulterated horror. His chest heaved, blood frothing at his lips, his eyes wide with the shock of a god who had just discovered he was mortal.
He had poured everything he had, every ounce of his rage, every fragment of his power, into that blast, and he was watching it fail to do anything more than annoy the man below.
"How..." Theo gasped, the word breaking into a wet cough. "How the fuck... how are you still standing?"
"Adaptation," Rex said.
The word was simple. Final.
"Everything you have is going to work exactly once, Theo."
"The first time, I learn. The second time? The second time belongs to me.
Rex didn’t wait for a reply. He didn’t give Theo the chance to regroup or scream again.
He rose.
There was no dramatic flourish of wings, no shimmering display of flight magic. Instead, Rex activated the Gravity Manipulation’s personal gravity reduction.

The world seemed to drop away beneath him as he inverted his own relationship with mass. In less than two seconds, he shot upward from the street level, a human bullet streaking through the distorted air.
He covered forty-five meters with the flat, terrifying efficiency of a predator who had already calculated the distance and was simply moving to close the gap.
Theo didn’t wait for Rex to reach him. Panicked, his instincts screaming that his godhood was being stripped away, he lashed out.

He threw a temporal acceleration working at point-blank range, a desperate, concentrated burst of warped time designed to force Rex’s body to move faster than its own nervous system could handle, tearing muscle from bone through sheer velocity.
Rex took the full, brutal first contact effect.
For a moment, his body became a prisoner of its own speed. His heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped bird, each beat occurring at a frequency that threatened to shatter his sternum.

His synapses fired with such violent intensity that his vision blurred into a streak of meaningless colors. It was a jarring, sickening dissonance, the feeling of a machine being forced to run at ten times its rated capacity while the environment around it remained stagnant.
His blood felt like molten lead racing through his veins.
’New subexpression detected: Temporal Acceleration,’ the Adaptation hummed in his mind. ’Analyzing parameters...’
Four point one seconds.
Rex’s internal clock snapped back to standard. The acceleration was still howling around him, but it no longer had purchase on his biology.
He was a still point in a rushing river.
Rex closed the distance in a blur of motion.
He hit Theo.
This wasn’t a tactical strike. This wasn’t a calculated probe.
This was a fucking execution. Rex channeled the full, devastating output of his martial arts mastery, amplified by the forty-five meters of momentum he had built during his ascent.
He used telekinesis as the delivery mechanism, a focused lance of invisible force, and his own enhanced physical strength as the payload.
The impact sounded like two freight trains colliding. A wet, crunching sound reverberated through the air as Theo’s ribs shattered under the concentrated pressure.
Theo was launched backward through the sky like a broken doll, a trail of crimson blood spraying from his mouth as he hurtled away from the Nightwing household.
He sailed through the air for sixty meters before the temporal designation’s physical enhancement kicked in, forcing his body to absorb the kinetic energy in a managed force collapse.
He didn’t crash; he simply stopped, suspended in midair by his own power.
Then, Theo screamed something that wasn’t a word; it was a command to reality itself.
’Temporal Rewind.’

This was the crown jewel of Theo’s power. Not the crude destruction of the area distortion, not the simple stagnation of the stop, but the sophisticated, terrifying ability to force a targeted system to reverse its own history.
He aimed it directly at Rex, attempting to unravel the last few seconds of Rex’s existence, to revert his body to a state before the damage, before the movement, and before the confrontation.
Against most, it was a death sentence.
Against Rex, it was a paradox.

The Rewind tore into Rex’s timeline, seeking purchase to reverse his state. But Rex’s Infinite Regeneration was already running at maximum output, knitting flesh together faster than time could unmake it.
The Rewind located a target that was already constantly rebuilding itself. It was trying to undo something that refused to stay undone.
The two powers grinded against each other in a silent, metaphysical war, producing nothing but a null result, an attempt to erase a shadow that refused to disappear.
Inside Rex’s mind, the adaptation screamed warnings. This was the most technically sophisticated expression of the temporal class it had ever encountered.
The analysis was painstakingly slow, incredibly complex, and utterly deadly.
’Analysis time: Six point two seconds.’
Six point two seconds of vulnerability.
Theo, sensing the window, didn’t waste a heartbeat. He knew the Rewind was failing to erase Rex, so he used the application time to launch a physical assault.
Emboldened by his divine designation, Theo tore through the air, closing the gap with inhuman speed.
His fist connected with Rex’s jaw with the force of a sledgehammer. The sound of bone splintering was audible even over the temporal howling.
Rex’s head snapped sideways, blood erupting from his split lip and torn cheek. A moment later, another strike, a kick to the ribs, sent a fresh spray of crimson across the hovering debris.
The damage was undeniable. It was raw and brutal.
But as fast as the blood flowed, it stopped. As fast as the bones cracked, they fused.
The Infinite Regeneration consumed the damage as quickly as Theo could inflict it, the flesh knitting shut in real time beneath the bruises.
Rex emerged from the six-second window with his jaw set and his eyes colder than the void. The adaptation was complete.
His coverage now included the ability to express temporal rewinds.
Rex rose in the air, stabilizing himself thirty meters away from the panting, blood-soaked Theo.
"Last category," Rex said. His voice was flat, devoid of anger, carrying only the terrifying certainty of an inevitable conclusion.
"How many times do I have to fucking say it?" Theo shrieked.

The controlled, measured delivery of his earlier grievances was gone. This was the raw, unhinged voice of a man who had been stripped of every defense, standing naked before a truth he couldn’t comprehend.
"He is not what you think he is! He is not what any of you fucking think he is!"
Theo’s eyes were wild, pleading, and murderous all at once.
Rex looked at him, his gaze unblinking.
"I know what he is," Rex said.

This was the most technically sophisticated expression of the temporal class it had ever encountered.
The analysis was painstakingly slow, incredibly complex, and utterly deadly.
’Analysis time: Six point two seconds.’
Six point two seconds of vulnerability.
Theo, sensing the window, didn’t waste a heartbeat.
He knew the Rewind was failing to erase Rex, so he used the application time to launch a physical assault.
Emboldened by his divine designation, Theo tore through the air, closing the gap with inhuman speed.
His fist connected with Rex’s jaw with the force of a sledgehammer.
The sound of bone splintering was audible even over the temporal howling.
Rex’s head snapped sideways, blood erupting from his split lip and torn cheek.
A moment later, another strike, a kick to the ribs, sent a fresh spray of crimson across the hovering debris.
The damage was undeniable.
It was raw and brutal.
But as fast as the blood flowed, it stopped.
As fast as the bones cracked, they fused.
The Infinite Regeneration consumed the damage as quickly as Theo could inflict it, the flesh knitting shut in real time beneath the bruises.
Rex emerged from the six-second window with his jaw set and his eyes colder than the void.
The adaptation was complete.
His coverage now included the ability to express temporal rewinds.
Rex rose in the air, stabilizing himself thirty meters away from the panting, blood-soaked Theo.
"Last category," Rex said.
His voice was flat, devoid of anger, carrying only the terrifying certainty of an inevitable conclusion.
"How many times do I have to fucking say it?" Theo shrieked.
The controlled, measured delivery of his earlier grievances was gone.
This was the raw, unhinged voice of a man who had been stripped of every defense, standing naked before a truth he couldn’t comprehend.
"He is not what you think he is!
He is not what any of you fucking think he is!"
Theo’s eyes were wild, pleading, and murderous all at once.
Rex looked at him, his gaze unblinking.
"I know what he is," Rex said.

chapters.title: Chapter 1049. Effectiveness Stripped of Its Moral Packaging
paragraphs: Theo stared at Rex, his chest heaving, blood dripping from his chin onto the shattered pavement below. The raw, unhinged fury in his eyes flickered for a moment, replaced by something more desperate: a need for validation, for someone to acknowledge the horror of what they were witnessing.
"Then what is he?" Theo demanded, his voice cracking, raw with a plea that he refused to voice. "If he’s not what I say he is, then what the fuck is he?"
Rex didn’t answer immediately. He hung suspended in the air, backlit by the flickering, unstable reality of the temporal storm.

He looked at Theo with the flat, patient attention of a professor observing a student who had failed a fundamental theorem, the kind of look that wasn’t angry but worse: it was disappointed in the student’s lack of comprehension.
"He is the most effective person you have encountered in your life," Rex said.
The words were delivered with a terrifying, clinical calm. "Which is not the same thing as being good."
"You are confusing effectiveness for virtue, Theo."
"You see him achieving results and you assume there is a moral compass guiding him."
"You are disoriented because you are seeing effectiveness stripped of its traditional moral packaging."
Theo flinched as if struck. "He is not your ally, Rex!"
"Can’t you see?! He is using you! He is using all of us as tools for whatever game he’s playing."
"I know," Rex said.
The simplicity of the answer seemed to physically wound Theo. His expression twisted a nauseating cascade of betrayal, rage, and confusion.
"I know," Rex repeated, his register unchanged. "I have known from the beginning."
"The people who are effective at the level I am observing do not act out of altruism."
"They have reasons for their effectiveness that they rarely present to those they intend to use."
"Their motives are not their methods."
Rex drifted closer, his shadow stretching across the distorted ground. "The question isn’t whether he is using us, Theo."
"That is a settled fact. The question is whether the usage produces outcomes that are preferable to the alternatives."
"And so far, the outcomes have been preferable to the alternatives. In the calculus of survival, utility outweighs intent."
This was the most dangerous version of Rex. He wasn’t the warm, social mask he wore to navigate human spaces, nor was he merely the cold weapon of combat.

This was the Philosopher Predator, the version that spoke the most brutal truths with the same casual detachment as he did the weather. He made the truth indistinguishable from a performance, which meant you could never truly know where the man ended and the machine began.
Theo turned away, unable to meet that gaze. His eyes wandered past the immediate crater of their battle, looking down at the city below.

The area affected by the temporal distortion was still hemorrhaging power at its edges. Beyond the immediate devastation of the Nightwing household, the city streets were caught in a nauseating, low-intensity flicker.

Buildings seemed to shudder, their surfaces blurring between new stone and ancient decay. The civilians in those buildings weren’t dead, but they were trapped in a state of profound existential nausea, their minds unable to anchor themselves to a single moment as their timelines wavered.
And then, Theo saw them.
The bodies.
People were collapsing in the streets, clutching their heads as their equilibrium shattered. This was the unintended consequence of a god-tier power being wielded by an untrained hand.
Theo had been focused on Rex on the immediate threat and had failed to manage the secondary hemorrhaging of his own power. He hadn’t intended the collateral damage.
He hadn’t intended for the disoriented screams to occur.
Rex watched Theo’s face crumble as he realized the scale of his failure.
The distortion was affecting children.

Rex’s Soul Manipulation allowed him to see what the naked eye could not. In the outer radius, where the temporal field was weaker, the children weren’t aging backward visibly, but their very essence was being frayed.
Their cellular timelines not yet fully established, still in the vulnerable process of forging a consistent identity, were being caught in the temporal eddies.
Their soul signatures showed a specific, haunting dimming: the mark of a child who had lost precious, irreplaceable moments of development to a random act of cosmic violence.
They were losing time they would never get back.
Rex did not say this to Theo. He did not offer comfort or condemnation.
He simply watched.
He let Theo stare at the collapsing civilians. He let Theo process the horrifying reality that his quest for justice had become an engine of random, senseless suffering.
He watched the realization sink in that his power was not a scalpel but a sledgehammer that could not distinguish between villain and innocent.
And then Rex watched Morwenna.
She had recovered with a terrifying speed, her system designation allowing her to reassemble her biological coherence faster than any normal human.
She pushed herself up from the rubble, blood still staining her clothes, and turned her gaze toward the city. She saw the flickering buildings.
She saw the people collapsing in the distance. She saw the horror of the uncontrolled field.
Rex watched her realize exactly what Theo had done.

Morwenna pushed herself upright, the movement sending fresh waves of agony through her healing tissues. Her muscles screamed as they reknitted, each cellular repair a painful reminder of the violence she had just endured.
Her gaze swept past the cratered earth, past the wreckage of the Nightwing household, and locked onto the city below.
She saw the flickering. She saw the nauseating stutter of reality.
And then she saw the bodies of the civilians who had simply folded like marionettes with their strings cut.
Her eyes moved to Theo.

He was suspended in the air, a broken god caught in the aftermath of his own catastrophe. The amber-gold aura that surrounded him, once a crisp, terrifying manifestation of absolute control, had begun to hemorrhage.

The edges of his power were no longer sharp; they had become diffuse and frayed, bleeding into the atmosphere like ink in water. It was the unmistakable signature of a mind that had broken someone whose attention had been violently severed from their focus, leaving their power to run on hollow momentum rather than conscious direction.
"Theo," Morwenna said.
Her voice wasn’t the warm authority of the matriarch, nor was it the soothing cadence she used to calm the wounded. It was something sharper, colder.
It was the voice of someone speaking to the raw, terrified human beneath the divine designation, the man who had spent twenty-nine years trying to hold back the tide of his own nature.
"Theo, look at what you are doing."
Theo didn’t move. His gaze remained fixed on the distant streets where the innocent were collapsing, his eyes reflecting the same horror she felt blooming in her own chest.
He looked like a man watching his own hands commit a murder he couldn’t stop.
He was still staring into that abyss when the air itself seemed to solidify.
Apollo arrived.
There was no thunderclap, no dramatic shockwave that would have marked a full-scale engagement. This was different.

This was a controlled descent, the arrival of a predator who had assessed the situation from miles away and chosen the most efficient method of approach. He came from the direction of the Academy, his energy signature humming at a measured, disciplined frequency.
He wasn’t here to destroy; he was here to manage.

He touched down on the cracked earth with the silent grace of a predator, his eyes immediately scanning the devastation. His gaze swept over the temporal distortion field, still flickering like a dying lightbulb.
Then his eyes moved to Theo, suspended and shattered.
Then to Rex, standing in the eye of the storm with unsettling stillness.
Finally, Apollo’s gaze landed on the outer radius of the people collapsed in the streets, the victims of a power that had outgrown its master.
"What happened to those people?" Apollo asked.
His voice wasn’t directed at Theo. He knew Theo was beyond answering.

Instead, Apollo turned his piercing stare toward Rex. He recognized Rex as the constant, the one standing at the epicenter of the information, the one who remained functional while everything else spiraled into chaos.
Rex didn’t flinch. His expression remained as impassive as marble.

"The temporal distortion’s field application at scale has secondary effects on biological systems," Rex said, his voice carrying the clinical detachment of an autopsy report. "The effects are severity graded by proximity and by the biological system’s developmental state."
The silence that followed was heavy, suffocating.
"The children," Apollo said, his voice dropping an octave, laced with something that sounded dangerously like restrained fury.
"The children at the outer radius have experienced some temporal rollback," Rex answered without hesitation. "Not large enough for visible physical change."
"The field at that distance lacks the concentration required for macro-scale aging."
"However, the effect has manifested at the cellular development timeline level... Their biological clocks have been disrupted."

Apollo’s eyes locked onto Rex’s. In that moment, the air between them grew cold, charged with the unspoken implications of Rex’s words: that this wasn’t just an accident but a mathematical inevitability of the power Theo had unleashed.
